The Aventon Solterra 3. (Photo: Aventon)

Riding a bike, at its heart, is amazing because it’s so simple. Two wheels, a frame, and suddenly you’re zooming around and discovering that going places can be fun . That’s why fixed-gear and single-speed bikes have such passionate fans: They prioritize the freedom that comes from embracing simplicity. With less weight and extraneous features, biking reenters the realm of play, and a daily commute or jaunt to grab groceries can feel a lot like flying.

Enter Aventon’s Soltera 2.5 and Soltera 3 ADV, which capture that fixie magic. The brand launched its legendary fixed gear Mataró model back in 2013, and that minimalist spirit infuses this new pair of e-bikes. They both marry a light-is-right sensibility with powerful but barely-there motors, all of it in a stealth design that will change the way you think about e-bikes.

The Class 1 Soltera 3 ADV Ebike ($1,499) will delight purists. Powered by a 250-watt (500-watt peak) motor, it offers 40 Nm of torque and a 70-mile range in a featherweight 37-pound package. It swaps a clanky chain for a carbon reinforced polymer belt that’s way easier to maintain and can last two to three times longer than any chain. Its single-speed configuration keeps you nimble and agile in the stop-start flow and narrow corridors you’ll encounter in urban traffic.

The Soltera 3’s updated geometry sings in the concrete maze, too—and everywhere. A longer wheelbase and lower bottom bracket keep it planted and predictable at speed, while a taller stack puts you in a more upright position that’s easier on your back, wrists, and neck on longer rides. A lower standover makes it easy to hop on and off at every light. With its ease of use and maintenance, there’s no simpler way to get some electric oomph into your daily ride.

Want to go down the zen road of simplicity but retain a bit more flex and options? You want the Soltera 2.5 Ebike ($1,199). For a scant 9 more pounds, you get a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain, on-demand throttle, wired features, and a 46-mile range. It brings a more traditional city e-bike feel while paring away the fluff to maintain fixie-forward geometry and feel.

Swapping your trusty-rusty analog commuting horse for an e-bike can feel like settling for an underpowered motorcycle. But both Soltera models deliver electric power while reaching back to a style of riding with less weight, complication, and stress—and more of what you need to make city streets fun to ride.

Aventon Bikes is here to inspire adventures, both big and small, in all terrains of life. No matter what we look like now, a year from now, or a decade from now, this is what keeps us moving forward. Redefine adventure and learn more at aventon.com .

Finding the right gear for the gravel cyclist in your life is notoriously difficult—mostly because their wish list never ends. Fortunately, we at Velo spend the entire year testing this equipment, so we know exactly what they actually need for a new year of adventures.

To help get the right gear into the right hands, I have put together a curated list of thirteen top-tier gravel gifts. This list covers a broad price range, features items that will impress even the rider who has it all, and includes a few deals to save you some cash along the way.

The Wolf Tooth DEL pedals are a piece of kit I cannot recommend enough—they are one of the few things I never ride gravel without. I use both the standard-issue alloy version and the premium Mark Zero titanium models. Both offer massive upside, making mountain bike shoes feel as efficient as road shoes on the flats, while remaining fully capable in mud, dirt, and ice.

Speaking of gravel staples, most of my rides with those pedals have been done in the Quoc Gran Tourer XC shoes. I have long been a fan of Quoc’s dedicated off-road line, and that hasn’t changed with this slightly stiffer XC version. While they might lack some of the hyper-stiffness of dedicated cross-country race shoes, the Gran Tourer is a 10/10 on the comfort scale and has proven to be incredibly durable. They are the perfect companion for everything from a three-hour adventure ride to a multi-day bikepacking trip.

Bikepacking is one of those things that people rarely do just once. If you are up for one trip, you’ll be up for the next one. A great rear rack only makes that more certain, and there are no rear racks quite like Tailfin. The only knock on Tailfin up until now has been the price. With the Journey Pannier Rack, the UK-based adventure brand finally has something at a lower price point. Now, you can get the same mix of functionality and craftsmanship that Tailfin has refined from working with the best ultra-riders in the world at a much-reduced price.

If you ride gravel, chances are you have been “darked on”—caught out too late without enough light to get you home. The Exposure Lights Sirius front light is built so this never happens again. This small light is brighter than it looks, easy to charge, and with the right mount, it stows safely out of the way to keep modern cockpits looking clean. Its industrial design adds a bit of bling to your setup, blending high-end functionality with a slick metallic aesthetic.

I never ride without a Dynaplug tool. For five years now, I have brought at least one of these small tools to fix flats on road, mountain, and gravel rides. It has saved me on a bikepacking trip through Ecuador and while road riding around my neighborhood. It doesn’t fix every flat, but dang, it will fix a lot of them. Most of that riding has been done with the exact same Dynaplug Racer Pro tool. So while the price seems high for one small tool, it is well worth it for any rider—especially gravel cyclists.

The Lezyne E-Drive pump has been an effective travel companion for me this year. It lets you inflate tires to precise pressures before riding, yet still fits in saddlebags big and small. It holds a charge well and, crucially, works with TPU tubes, which is key for long trips where you’re more likely to need a tube to save the day.

This might be a product of where I live, but on many gravel rides, the sun is the enemy. Long dirt roads often don’t offer a ton of shade, and the Velans 2 sunglasses from Sungod have been fantastic partners. The coverage is excellent, but they still breathe well at slower speeds. I have dropped them, shoved them in pockets, and sat on them, and they have survived without a single scratch to show for it.

Gravel clothing has a bunch of definitions. For some, it’s skinsuits and aero socks. For others, it’s baggy shorts and tech tees. Yet, for most, it’s just bibs and jerseys that work well for long rides. The Gobik CX Pro jersey hits the bullseye in this regard. It is a breathable, race-cut jersey that still fits exceptionally well. Best of all, the splash of color pops against everything from desert landscapes to dark forests, helping you stay visible to the few cars driving down odd dirt roads.

While I tend to skew toward the lycra side of the gravel clothing divide, I have loved this baggy piece of cycling kit for years. These versatile and breathable pants are great for everything from a long dirty day to travel, as the ventilation and zippered pockets are just as fantastic for the airplane as they are for the bike. I have two pairs, and I find myself gravitating toward them more and more as a comfortable alternative to leg warmers or tights on colder off-road adventures.

No matter what I do, I cannot quite kick drip lube as a part of my gravel cycling. Yes, hot melt tools like the Silca Chain Waxing System are highly effective, but they don’t fully stand on their own. Even a well-waxed chain occasionally needs a refresh on a trip. Out of all the options I have tried, I have found that Faast Chain Lube does the trick best. It lasts a long time, handles grit well, and feels very smooth. It even pairs perfectly with a Silca wax base if you prefer to use a hybrid system.…

Polygon's new Tambora gravel bike. (Photo: Polygon Bikes)

Since 1989, manufacturing and development has been in Polygon Bikes’ DNA. The Indonesia-based factory brand is in a country shaped by tremendous geological forces. The island nation’s massive volcanoes have reformed the landscape countless times and created awe-inspiring topography.

The lesson: Change is good. Polygon focused on a clear priority with the evolution of the all-new Tambora: speed. This is the fastest gravel bike the company has produced, with design elements that let riders push their routes faster and further than ever. Compared to the previous version of the Tambora, the front end is 32mm lower, while the head angle slackens by 0.8 degrees. Those tweaks improve aerodynamics for both bike and rider, while the longer wheelbase and chainstays create more stability when you’re charging down the trail.

​Adding to the Tambora’s race-ready performance: its frame. The frame’s ACX carbon-fiber construction takes inspiration from its Helios road bike sibling—designed to excel at power transfer while reducing ride fatigue. The bike also boasts 55c tire clearance and is compatible with 1x and 2x drivetrains. If more rugged terrain calls to you, the Tambora is also compatible with aftermarket suspension forks up to 40mm of travel, without changing the current geometry.

​While speed is this bike’s specialty, it also features the thoughtful, rider-friendly design elements Polygon is known for. The new Tambora takes full advantage of the brand’s PolyPocket internal frame storage, which offers a full downtube width opening for easy access. This soft-sided, zippered pouch holds tools, snacks, and other essentials in a convenient, low-profile package. Up in the cockpit, a Fidlock mount recessed into the top tube makes it quick and easy to connect your preferred accessories, while keeping everything tight when you ratchet up the RPMs.

Also great: The value proposition for Polygon Bikes is as good as the performance. The Tambora series starts at $1,799, with a wide range of competitively priced options. The Tambora 7 Di2 ($2,999) and Tambora 9 AXS with SRAM Force ($4,499) are particularly good deals considering the specs.

Put it all together and you have a bike that’s both fast and capable of serious saddle time—and comes at sweet price. With four models across six frame sizes, there’s a redesigned Tambora for every gravel rider who wants to experience the wonders of evolution for themselves.

Founded in 1989, Polygon began with a simple belief: Great bikes shouldn’t be out of reach. What started as a small OEM operation has grown through decades of building, experimenting, and refining bikes for real riders—experiences that still define the global brand today.

Today, State is launching the 6061 All-Road V2, and it packs a ton of value into an alloy frame. Of course, the price jumps out as the biggest draw, but the bike also brings 55mm of clearance, improved componentry, and truly progressive geometry. Progressive geometry that many big brands say they provide, yet ultimately don’t quite hit.

For State, this new geometry is built around stability and traction, complete with a slightly slacker headtube angle, a long 445mm chainstay length, and a 73mm bottom bracket drop. State also tweaks the geometry on a size-by-size basis, which aims to maintain similar handling across the size run. Crucially, for the smaller sizes, this size-based geometry is designed to reduce toe overlap—even for 55mm tires on a 48cm frame.

The 6061 All-Road v2 is firmly pitched as a budget bike that brings costs down through components and materials, yet tries to bring quality through intentional design. That is where those aspects of geometry have come in.

Since the bike is not race-focused, that has given State the license to zero in on a geometry that boosts stability through the front and rear of the bike. Instead of packing big tires into a short chassis, State took a chance to push the expectations around head tube angle and chainstay length. This length, specifically the head tube angle ranging from 70-71.5 degrees and a 445 mm chainstay, is going to add stability—especially with the larger tires—and is designed to balance weight distribution for better traction. These attributes make a ton of sense for an entry-level bike.

Nevertheless, viewing this as an entry-level bike does do a bit of a disservice to how this bike could grow with a rider. From aspects like a T47 bottom bracket to relatively aero-shaped tubing with semi-internal cable routing, the bike could be upgraded easily.

Like all of State’s budget builds, part of how the brand finds savings is through building bikes with drivetrain components from outside of Shimano and SRAM. In the past, this has led to some, erm, creative component selection.

One of the most frustrating examples of this, in my experience, was a hybrid braking system that combined cable-actuated levers with a hydraulic caliper. It created one of the most disjointed, frustrating brake systems I have ever used, but it’s gone. On this new build, the system is a full flat-mount hydraulic system that should make for much more consistent and digestible riding.

There are still quirks like a Sensah SRX Pro 1×12 rear mech and a State-branded 42t crankset, but the frame is both UDH-compatible and has reasonable 165mm cranks for the smaller sizes and 170mm for the larger frames. The bike also comes with the option to run both 700c and 650b wheel sizes.

Lastly, speaking of those wheels, State has an in-house 700c wheel option that has an updated 25mm internal width, 32-spoke count rim to suit the wide 50mm Continental Hard Pack tires that come stock with the bike. There is also the option to upgrade to the DT Swiss G 1800 or the Zipp 303 S XPLR wheelset.

The State 6061 All-Road v2 is available in three colors—Liquid Emerald, Chrome Red, and Metallic Smoke—and four sizes. The builds start at $1,499, with add-ons including wheels, pedals, saddles, seatpost, and bottle cages.

For more information or to configure yours, visit State’s website .

Stinner Frameworks has a lot more wheels to build with. The metal frame builder based in Santa Barbara has launched Stoic Components, a sub-brand within the company, to manufacture carbon wheels built to match the bikes in Stinner’s catalog.

The component brand is a long time in the making for Stinner. In the press release, Stinner said the brand has been in the making for a decade, stemming from a collaboration with Jones Wheel’s late founder John Jones.

“John and I planned to start a component brand together,” Aaron Stinner, the founder of Stinner Frameworks, said. We lost him to cancer in 2021, before we got the chance. Stoic Components is that brand. We’re starting where he would have: carbon wheels, each matched to a Stinner frame and laced to Stoic hubs.”

Each wheelset will start at $1,499 and use the same basic ingredients: Pillar PSR Triple Butted J-bend spokes, Toray T700/T800 carbon, and in-house hubs. The wheels also have a 265-pound rider weight limit, sealed cartridge bearings, and specific asymmetric rim profiles.

Beyond the new wheels, Stinner has also unveiled a collection of other updates. The Stinner Select range of bikes now uses higher-quality Columbus Life tubing and improved specs. Stinner Select 2.0 framesets will now cost $2,599, while complete builds start at $5,499.

Additionally, if you have wondered how I capture my bike imagery, I have been a long-time user of Stinner’s Photo Stick. The small titanium tool is built to easily prop a bike up for photos while packing down small enough to fit in a carry-on bag or a rear pocket. It uses a three-point construction to provide a strong lean point to prop the bike up wherever seems fit.

Stinner has released a new Photo Stick 2.0, also called the Photostique, which is available now for $109.99 MSRP.

To learn more about the Stoic Component wheels or the brand’s other upgrades, check out Stinner’s website .

This week, the full crew is together to do some arguing. Host Mike Levy, Lisa Charlebois, Logan Jones-Wilkins, and I (Josh Ross, though Blue Hat Guy works too) are debating Zwift versus everyone and whether 32-inch wheels are actually here to stay.

Before we get to the main event, we dive into a pile of listener comments from last week’s indoor riding and Zwift Plus discussion. That includes everything from TrainerRoad or Strava versus Zwift (and why fearing for life on rollers might be the best way) to whether Zwift will eventually fold Rouvy into a single platform. For the record, I’m putting my prediction on the board now: Rouvy ceases to exist as a separate thing in three years. We also tackle a listener theory that virtual cars in Zwift video routes are desensitizing indoor-first riders to real traffic—a take that leaves Mike and me pretty much speechless before Logan steps in with a much more reasonable explanation.

From there, it is time for the topic everyone loves to hate: 32-inch gravel wheels. Logan just wrapped up 500 miles on the MMosaic GT i55 32—a custom titanium bike built around a proper 32-inch carbon fork—and he is a huge fan. He argues it makes gravel riding noticeably more fun, with better rollover, more traction, and geometry that actually makes sense off-road. Mike agrees, arguing that the best thing about 32-inch wheels isn’t even the wheels themselves, but the longer, more stable geometry they force frame builders to adopt.

I am on the other side of the fence. While I don’t doubt the off-road performance gains exist, my argument is a business one: consumers have wheel-size fatigue, brands don’t want to manage multiple standards, and 32-inch gravel bikes are headed for the same fate as 650b within five years. That leads to a back-and-forth over whether brands can actually pull off two wheel sizes across a single frame run (when they still struggle to spec the right handlebar widths), whether 700c gravel bikes are just turning into “all-road” bikes, and what all of this means for shorter riders who don’t want to feel like they’re riding a monster truck.

Lisa: “This is gonna sound so dumb. I’m sorry, everybody. But it looks like you’re on a Big Wheel… It just looks so weird. The scale is so wrong.” Mike: “We all look so weird. We’re wearing spandex riding bicycles around, talking about watts and carbs. We look stupid and I love it.” Logan: “You know how many people noticed I was riding 32 at Big Sugar? Zero people. Nobody noticed.” Lisa: “Yeah, but you’re tall, dude. You look in proportion.”

As always, let us know where you land in the comments—are you with Logan on the 32-inch future, or are you siding with Blue Hat Guy? And make sure to vote in this week’s poll below to tell us whether you’re actually planning to buy a 32-inch gravel bike when they hit the market in force.

SBT GRVL has been embroiled in online controversy after an uproar over the brand’s enforcement of a trademark around the term GRVL.

It all started with an Instagram post. @rezgravel on Instagram, the page representing an Indigenous-led community gravel event in Sacaton, Arizona, posted an email they received from SBT GRVL requesting that Rez Gravel stop using the term GRVL in marketing materials around the event.

The Rez Gravel post was a protest of that email. The post comment highlighted the lack of infrastructure around the Rez Gravel event, how the email from SBT would force them to spend money they don’t have on new posters and a logo redesign, and criticism of the lack of care and consideration SBT GRVL showed in denying their request for comped entry into SBT GRVL for native riders in the past.

That post generated over a thousand likes and hundreds of comments, with many people criticizing SBT GRVL, bringing into question the viability of a trademark of the term GRVL, and supporting the Indigenous-led event and organization.

On Sunday, November 15th, Rez Gravel posted a screenshot of an email the race received from SBT GRVL around the use of the GRVL term on previous marketing material for their January 9th and 10th community bike rides.

“So I guess @sbtgrvl owns ‘GRVL’ and we’ll have to stop using GRVL,” the caption under Rez Gravel’s post read. “SBT GRVL introduced me to gravel cycling when I was an @rideforracialjustice RFRJ athlete in 2022. In the past, I have been one of SBT GRVL’s biggest supporters. I returned to SBT GRVL in 2023, 2024 and in 2023 even went halfway around the world to support their race @fnldgrvl FNLD GRVL in Finland.

“I tried to bring a Native Gravel team to SBT GRVL in 2024. I tried to ask Amy, Ryan, and Greer for free or even discounted entry as a way to honor the First Nations people, including my cousin from the Ute Indian Tribe- Uintah and Ouray Reservation, whose people were removed from the land in the area now known as Steamboat Springs. Amy and her team refused to honor native people with even a reduced-fee entry for my cousin in 2024.”

And then came the crux of their argument.

“Rez Gravel does not use the GRVL in our LLC, DBA, or website names. Rez Gravel does not sell any merchandise that uses the GRVL name or logo. Rez Gravel is owned by a Gila River Indian Community tribal member and solely operates on the Gila River Indian Community a Sovereign Nation.

“Rez Gravel only has an annual revenue of around $4,000, and after expenses only about 2,000-3,000 keeps our community bike shop going for the year. The posters are printed for 2027 and out of money until some more funds come in from 2027 Registration.”

A second post from the Rez Gravel organization a day later added to that online discourse, with the organization posting details of the federally registered trademarks that SBT GRVL invoked in their emails and a caption that articulated how the Rez Gravel organization was not infringing upon the two separate trademarks that SBT GRVL has around the term GRVL.

In total, SBT GRVL has trademarks on the terms SBT GRVL, FNLD GRVL, RADL GRVL, and two specific trademarks around the term GRVL. One of those terms covers cycling events, while the other protects the use of GRVL for merchandise.

In the case of Rez Gravel, SBT GRVL didn’t specify which trademark they were invoking—they did not have to since the email was a courtesy note and not a formal cease—but it is likely the trademark around the event.

In an exclusive interview with Velo , the SBT GRVL organizers explained the reason behind the email and their trademarks.

“It was back a few years ago that we decided that we needed to trademark the event,” Amy Charity, the SBT GRVL race director, told Velo.

“We had established a brand, and we knew that SBT GRVL stood for something that we were really proud of. We were a safe event, an event that was inclusive, an event that was credible and professional.

“At the time, we were also considering expanding our brand by putting on events such as FNLND GRVL or RADL GRVL. In doing so, we wanted to ensure that the riders, the participants, and the sponsors would know what they were getting—when you hear GRVL, when you see GRVL, there’s a standard that you associate with what we will uphold and what we’ll honor.”

Like all trademark processes, that trademark process took many months to complete with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). In that process, to get the trademarks for the term GRVL, SBT GRVL had to both prove distinctiveness and prove they were using the trademark to identify their brand to consumers.

Additionally, as with all trademark or copyright instances, SBT GRVL had to demonstrate they were actively using the trademark for commercial use, and that they are actively enforcing their intellectual property if they deem that trademark has been violated.

That has meant that each time an event has used the GRVL distinction since, they have been required by law to notify the brand that is using their trademarked term.

“The very first time it happened, it was because there was confusion in the marketplace,” Ryan Steers, SBT GRVL’s Marketing Director, told Velo. “We had a sponsor approach us and say, we didn’t know that you were putting on an event in a different country, and asked why we didn’t tell them we were doing it and why they weren’t the first that you approached.

“It was confusing, especially in our market, particularly because it was a US-based company putting on an international event with GRVL in the title. So we reached out to that event business and said, ‘Hey, we wanted to give you a heads-up, we own the trademark for GRVL as it relates to events.’

“That’s what we do when we see an event out there related to gravel cycling that has been using GRVL. There have been around three events that we’ve reached out to.”…

In 2027, the US will have two new UCI gravel races, with Borderlands Gravel the latest to join the UCI’s selection of sanctioned gravel races. The race in Douglas, Arizona, runs along the far southeastern border of Arizona and Mexico, with a short stint in New Mexico along the way.

The 2026 edition took place on November 14th, and Velo was on-site to get a sense of the unique event that melds the area’s American and Mexican identities.

Next year, the race will use the same terrain, but with more at stake as it will be one of three UCI Gravel World Series stops in the United States. BWR Utah in Cedar City will be the other new addition to the UCI calendar, while Highlands Gravel returns for another year.

The course, which will be an early qualifier for the 2028 UCI Gravel World Championship, will be an 87-mile largely out-and-back course with 5,000 feet of climbing. Half of the route runs directly along sections of the border wall, with the race using the gravel service road that cuts through high desert vistas, washes, and creosote fields.

The second half of the out-and-back leaves the border behind and climbs its way up one of the “sky islands” of Arizona. The climbing is gradual at first, with 14 miles at 2%, before a 1.6-mile, 8% wall that crests just shy of 6,000 feet of altitude.

The elements will only add to the challenge of the day. This year, it was mud and wind that challenged the riders, with rare November rains soaking the course. In other years, heat and sand could play a factor.

The constant factor? The gravel road that cuts through the Coronado National Forest in the New Mexico portion of the out-and-back is some of the most spectacular gravel riding I have encountered this year.

From a racing perspective, Borderlands Gravel will continue to be one of the last gravel races of the year, and thus one of the first opportunities to qualify for the next UCI Gravel World Championship in AlUla, Saudi Arabia, giving riders nearly a year to prepare for the event.

The Ari Bikes Shafer HP (Photo: Ari Bikes)

Let’s be honest: if you could have infinite bikes, you probably would. Unfortunately, most of us tend to be limited by our savings accounts, our garage space, and our significant other’s desire that we spend our money on literally anything else. That’s when an elegant all-arounder like the Ari Bikes Shafer comes in.

Part race bike, part gravel rig, part long-distance hauler, the all-carbon Shafer was designed to meld high-tech performance with backcountry durability. Better yet, it actually delivers. The first jaw-dropper is the weight. The Shafer’s featherlight carbon frame clocks in at just 2 pounds—nearly a half-pound lighter than previous generations—and yet has enough clearance for 700×58c / 29×2.25-inch tires. That means riders can line up at a race one day, then slap on some fat tires and disappear into the woods the next.

Weather-sealed downtube storage, tons of frame and fork mounts, and internal dynamo routing give bikepackers and ultra-distance riders the features they need to go further. Meanwhile, dropper-post and suspension fork compatibility (up to 60 mm) means you can tackle rough trails without having to swap out for a dedicated mountain bike. Five complete build options let you further dial in the components and suspension to your specific needs, and each bike is custom-built to the rider’s measurements. Fancy, huh?

At this point, your mind might be wandering back to that crucial first point on our list of bike-accumulation obstacles: expense. While everything about Shafer—from its sleek geometry to its high-fashion paint job—screams high-performance, the hang tag isn’t what you might expect from a custom build. In fact, the Shafer’s Sport model starts at just $2,549.

That accessible price point comes courtesy of Ari Bikes’s direct-to-consumer model. Every Ari is built, tuned, and test-ridden at the brand’s Utah headquarters. Cutting out the middlemen helps the brand dramatically slash overhead without sacrificing quality. Ari also backs its bikes with a lifetime frame warranty and a 30-day love-it-or-return-it guarantee.

Now let’s say you like the sound of all that, but there’s one more category you’re looking for in your all-arounder: pedal assist. Ari Bikes has an answer to that, too. The Shafer HP , a carbon-frame gravel e-bike, is an extension of the Shafer’s ride philosophy. It combines the same geometry and versatility with a lightweight, whisper-quiet electric motor that provides a natural-feeling assist on big climbs and longer rides. Whether you’re dialing in your fitness, committing to a long daily commute, or just trying to access different types of adventures, the Shafer HP gives you all the perks of the analog bike, but with way more precise control over your effort and speed.

With a 360 Watt-hour integrated battery and an optional 160 Watt-hour range extender, the Shafer HP can handle long days between charges. Meanwhile, its 700×58c tire clearance and suspension-fork and dropper compatibility give it all the rugged adventure performance of the original Shafer. Even better news: the basic model rings in at just $4,899—a steal given its outsized capability.

Yes, it would be fun to buy three or four more bikes this season. And if you’ve been looking for an excuse to dramatically expand your fleet, we’re sorry to say the Shafer isn’t going to help you build your case. But if you’re looking for a true quiver killer that’s going to help you save money, go further, and access just about every conceivable adventure on two wheels, well, you may have just met your new ride.

Ari Bikes is a Utah-based, direct-to-consumer brand selling bikes worldwide since 2005. Ari’s mission is to help people live better now by making exceptional bikes more accessible. Backed by a 4.9-star rating, Ari offers direct-to-rider pricing, custom setup, a lifetime and transferable warranty, and a love-it-or-return-it guarantee to help deliver on that mission.

An appeals court in Florence ended the criminal case against former road world champion Mario Cipollini on Thursday after ruling that the statute of limitations had expired on all counts.

Cipollini, 59, was facing a three-year prison term handed down by a Lucca court in 2022, Italian media reported .

The case began in 2017 when Cipollini’s ex-wife Sabrina Landucci filed a complaint. The charges included alleged domestic mistreatment, stalking, bodily harm, and threats.

Landucci reached a separate agreement with Cipollini over damages and withdrew from the proceedings, La Stampa reported.

“Today I can declare, without any fear of contradiction, that I am a citizen with a completely clean criminal record,” Cipollini wrote on Facebook.

He said his lawyers had challenged the Lucca court’s account of events, and that basically time had run out before an appeals court could hear a possible challenge.

Cipollini — nicknamed Il Re Leone (The Lion King) and Super Mario — retired in 2008 after a 20-year pro career. The flamboyant sprinter won the 2002 world title, 160 pro wins, Milan-San Remo , and a record 42 stage victories at the Giro d’Italia.

Cipollini often ran afoul with race organizers and the UCI for his outrageous antics, that included dressing up in a toga ahead of a stage at the Tour de France or racing in a zebra-print skin suit.

In 2008, he was linked to the Operación Puerto doping scandal, an allegation he denied. In 2013, the French Senate released a report that linked Cipollini as one of the riders whose samples from the 1998 Tour de France were positive for traces of EPO when retested in 2004.

Since retiring, Cipollini has remained in the public eye, with appearances on Italy’s version of “Dancing With The Stars” and other reality TV programs.

Cipollini launched his own bike brand in 2010 and November 2025 he underwent heart surgery in Ancona, Italian media reported last year.

Chloé Dygert may be leaving the WorldTour, but she’s keeping her foot on the accelerator with an ambitious target of three medals at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics .

Dygert told Velo she’s aiming to defend Team USA’s team pursuit title and chase the time trial and road race at LA 2028.

With the Games less than two years away, the 29-year-old is already building toward a possible gold medal trifecta that could make her one of the breakout stars in Los Angeles.

“Of course it would be great to win all three, the time trial for sure, and then the road race would be just a total bonus,” Dygert told Velo . “I gotta be realistic here, so winning the time trial and obviously coming back and winning the team pursuit would be huge.”

As one of America’s most successful Olympic cyclists , Dygert already owns four Olympic medals. She won team pursuit gold and time trial bronze at Paris 2024, adding to her team pursuit bronze from Tokyo 2020 and silver from Rio 2016.

Qualifying comes first. Then she has to hit her peak across two disciplines in the summer of 2028.

Speaking to Velo’s Hannah Knapp at El Tour de Tucson, Dygert was already putting down some training sessions on the outdoor track.

“So for how the Olympics works, it kind of goes by body count rather than like the event itself,” she said. “I’m for sure gonna do the track team pursuit as long as we qualify and then hopefully the time trial and then by doing the time trial, I have to do the road race, so I’ll be doing three events.”

Two medals in Paris, so why not three in Los Angeles?

Dygert’s road to Los Angeles will run through the United States.

This week she confirmed she’s returning to Virginia’s Blue Ridge TWENTY28 after six seasons with Canyon SRAM in the WorldTour.

Dygert has been through the wringer with injuries and health setbacks. Her time trial crash at the 2020 world championships in Imola, where she suffered a devastating injury to her left leg, still divides her career into before and after.

“I’ve spent my time in Europe and gave it the best shot that I could. Before my accident, that was the plan,” Dygert said. “I wanted to go to Europe and I wanted to win everything in Europe. I wanted to be the best in Europe.

“But because of the accident, unfortunately some of those goals got derailed. I think it was very obvious that I just was never going to be the athlete that I was before the accident.”

Dygert returns to Nicola Kramer’s Continental team where she raced as a junior a decade ago.

“So now it’s all about what do I do going forward, how do I make the best of who I can still be, and that is why I’ve decided to come back to America,” Dygert said.

“I’m coming back to something that I’m familiar with, coming back to a team that supports me and my goals,” she said. “I want to win the worlds. I want to win the Olympics, and I’ve done that before with her, and so what a better team to come back to.”

Dygert is one of USA Cycling’s best shots at gold on home roads in 2028.

The two-time world time trial champion took bronze against the clock in Paris, and she heads into the Los Angeles Olympics with a title to defend on the track and a third chance at a medal in the road race. Here’s how all three stack up.

1. Defend gold in the team pursuit Dygert has been at the heart of the U.S. team pursuit for three straight Olympics, with a medal each time and a breakthrough gold in Paris. She skipped the track worlds last month, but told Velo the pursuit is still front and center in her plans for LA28.

Team USA has work to do. The Americans finished ninth in qualifying at the Shanghai worlds, more than three seconds shy of advancing. Kristen Faulkner was the only rider from the Paris gold medal quartet on the start line in China.

Only eight teams will start in Los Angeles. Great Britain won gold in Shanghai ahead of Italy and Germany, a reminder of how deep the field is. The Americans will have to earn their place first.

If they can find their Paris speed again, they’ll be in the medal fight.

2. Win gold in the individual time trial This is her other big target.

Dygert has won two world time trial titles, and she was less than a second from Olympic silver on slick roads in Paris. Grace Brown was in a league of her own that day, beating Dygert by more than 90 seconds. Just 0.87 seconds separated Dygert from silver medalist Anna Henderson.

The course will matter. Organizers have confirmed a start at the LA Zoo and a finish at Griffith Observatory, with the full route still to come.

How much climbing comes before that finish could shape Dygert’s chances of turning bronze into gold.

3. Take a shot in the Olympic road race First, Dygert needs a spot on the road team.

The United States has two guaranteed road race places per gender as host and can earn up to four per gender through the UCI nations rankings.

The road race is the longest shot, but Dygert has the engine for a long, hard race in national colors.

She finished 31st in the Olympic road race in Tokyo and 15th in Paris. She was fourth in 2019 and second at the 2024 worlds in Zürich to show what she can do when she’s in the mix at the finish.

Besides that and maybe even more importantly, it is also known as the unofficial end-of-year celebration for the British bike industry. Surprisingly, there were even some new products on display, which is not always a given at Rouleur considering the time of year. One brand representative managed to summarize what most exhibitors were showcasing pretty well: brands were celebrating this year’s achievements, or teasing next year’s novelties.

Besides, with an Italian pavilion and many British bespoke brands attending too, there was more than enough to feast the eyes on. Let’s dive into our tech gallery of one of the last bike shows of the season.

When it comes to bike computers, the biggest players are Garmin and Wahoo, and each takes a fundamentally different approach to solving the same puzzle. If you want simple, Wahoo is the one for you, and all three size options are being offered at a massive discount right now.

Across the entire lineup, Wahoo makes the easiest-to-use bike computers on the market. They are the ultimate “it just works” devices: add your accounts, connect to Wi-Fi, and you’re ready to ride. You aren’t giving up serious metrics for that simplicity, either. Instead of painstakingly assigning data to individual boxes, you just list your fields in order of importance in the app and use the side buttons to zoom in or out on the fly. Even if you normally like a lot of data, it’s great to zoom in to just power and speed when it’s late in a ride, everything hurts, and you just need to pedal.

The main trade-off in the past was always that Wahoo doesn’t offer an all-encompassing 24/7 wearable ecosystem, but even that’s been fixed recently. Wahoo has a partnership with Coros, and if you want a full picture of both training and recovery, you can use the Coros backend system and a Coros watch seamlessly with your Wahoo computer.

At the top of the lineup sits the Elemnt Ace, which is Wahoo’s answer for riders who want maximum screen real estate and every feature the brand makes. It has a large 3.8-inch color touchscreen, 64GB of storage, dual-band GPS, a built-in speaker for voice turn-by-turn navigation, and up to 30 hours of claimed battery life. Its headline differentiator is an integrated wind sensor that measures live airspeed to quantify headwinds, tailwinds, and drafting. All of that hardware comes with a clear trade-off in size and weight—at 208 grams, it is noticeably larger and heavier than a standard head unit, which is why Wahoo includes an aluminum out-front mount in the box.

This is probably the one you really want. It keeps almost everything that makes the Ace appealing—including the 16-million-color touchscreen interface, 64GB of storage, dual-band GPS, and the built-in speaker for audible turn-by-turn prompts—while dropping the wind sensor and massive size. Instead of a 3.8-inch display, it steps down to a still very usable 2.8-inch screen and cuts the weight nearly in half to 109 grams, with a claimed battery life of up to 25 hours.

If you want something smaller and lighter for racing or just prefer a cleaner cockpit, the Elemnt Bolt 3 strips the formula down to the essentials. This is also the best budget play, but it’s still a very capable computer. Weighing in at 84 grams with a 2.3-inch color display, it drops both the touchscreen and the audio speaker, relying strictly on physical buttons for control. Storage drops to 32GB and claimed battery life dips to 20 hours, but you still get the same dual-band GPS, high-contrast color screen tech, and updated Ready-To-Ride interface found on its bigger siblings.

Everyone wants Paul Seixas . In 2027, they might get their chance.

Seixas’ contract expires after next season, and the mad scramble for his contract is already starting to rumble.

He’s not alone. Tom Pidcock , Sepp Kuss , and Lenny Martinez are the other marquee names off-contract in 2027 who will be headlining next year’s high-stakes transfer market.

A few riders are still looking for spots in 2027 after their deals ran out this year, including Primož Roglič and Max Schachmann, among a dozen others.

For everyone else, attention is already shifting to the 2027-28 transfer season, which could rival last year’s upheaval , when Remco Evenepoel, Juan Ayuso and Oscar Onley all ripped up existing deals and swapped jerseys.

Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard are both under contract and secure at the top of the hierarchy. For anyone else hoping to catch up, a few big names could make the difference.

For this year, it’s going to be all about the Seixas Sweepstakes. And what he does will shape the entire market .

The gossip will start at the team camps next month in Spain and be hyped by leaks, exclusives, and conjecture all the way to the Tour de France.

Here are the big transfer names to watch in 2027:

There won’t be a bigger transfer saga in 2027 than Paul Seixas. And there might not be a bigger price tag, either, if this year’s $13 million rumored offer comes true.

The 20-year-old French phenom more than proved his quality in a rock-solid WorldTour campaign, becoming the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia and nearly hitting the podium in his Tour de France debut with fourth overall.

He’s the top name off-contract in 2027, and nearly every team has reached out . Visma-Lease a Bike and Pinarello Q36.5 are already circling, with Q36.5 reportedly putting a massive €13 million per year on the table for 2028.

The bigger question is whether Decathlon can convince him to stay beyond 2027.

The team is certainly trying. It has recruited more stage racing support, notably Pavel Sivakov, to give its franchise rider more company when the road kicks up.

With suitors lining up, the ball is in his court. Seixas could name his price and take his pick, but salary might not settle this one.

Can Decathlon give him everything he needs in coaching, training, nutrition, equipment, and aerodynamics to match the super teams?

Keeping Seixas will take more than paying him like a Tour winner. The deciding factor will be if Decathlon can convince him he can become one there.

Visma will have nearly half its roster out of contract at the end of 2027, so the team will be busy locking down its leaders and shopping for fresh legs.

One rider it probably won’t have to worry about losing is Sepp Kuss. It’s hard to imagine the “Eagle of Durango” in any other jersey.

And he’s still putting numbers on the board, including a Giro stage win to complete the “grand tour” sweep of stages, and finishing fifth at the Vuelta.

Kuss admits he doesn’t like the pressure of leadership, so he probably won’t be chasing a big-money contract to be a GC leader on another team.

The bigger question might be how much longer Kuss wants to keep doing it.

A recent at-home video offered a glimpse of a happy life in Andorra with his wife and child. So far, there’s no hint he’s ready to trade mountain passes for more afternoons at home. His favored program of racing all three grand tours also fits his work-life balance.

If both sides want it, a “forever” contract like those signed by Wout van Aert and Marianne Vos would seem a fitting way to keep him in yellow and black.

It’s equally hard to imagine Pidcock going anywhere else.

His blockbuster move to Pinarello Q36.5 was one of the top transfers two years ago.

Pinarello Q36.5 remains one of the most aggressive teams on the rider market , picking up 10 new riders coming into 2027.

Doug Ryder, with the backing of team owners, is pushing the pedal for WorldTour classification by the next round at the end of 2028.

For Pidcock, his spot is secure, so it will be a question of hammering out the details on how many zeroes are attached to his next deal.

If it weren’t for Seixas, Lenny Martinez would have finished the 2026 Tour de France as the top French rider, in fifth.

That will give him some bargaining power coming into 2027.

At 23, his stock is still rising, even if Seixas has grabbed the spotlight as France’s next great Tour hope.

The son of Olympic mountain bike champion Miguel Martinez and grandson of Tour king of the mountains winner Mariano Martinez has the family pedigree. The consistency is still lacking, but the first half of 2026 confirmed his potential.…

Two of America’s most promising teens — Enzo Hincapie and Jack Klau — are moving up in the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe talent pipeline in 2027.

Hincapie, 18, steps up to the U23 Red Bull Rookies after winning the U.S. junior national title.

Klau, 17, signs with the U19 junior team grenke-Auto Eder.

That puts two Americans right in the center of Red Bull’s development train that runs directly from the junior team to the Rookies and on to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe WorldTour squad.

This is cycling’s version of getting drafted out of high school by the Yankees. Red Bull has one of the peloton’s biggest budgets and is betting big on development, but the odds are still long of hitting the WorldTour.

Could these two up end up as Remco Evenepoel’s teammate in a few years?

Red Bull rolled out its rosters for its two development squads for 2027, and the two Americans both get star billing.

Hincapie — the son of former pro George Hincapie — spent 2026 on Red Bull’s grenke-Auto Eder U19 squad. Standout rides include victory at the U.S. junior title and fourth at the junior Tour of Flanders.

Those results helped earn him one of four promotions from the junior squad to the Rookies for 2027.

That bump is significant because Red Bull is investing heavily on its development programs to build out its WorldTour team.

Four Red Bull Rookies from the U23 squad — Tour de l’Avenir winner Lorenzo Finn , Alessio Magagnotti, Davide Donati and Sebastian Putz — are graduating to Red Bull’s WorldTour lineup in 2027.

“In 2026 we had clear winners. In 2027 we are much more versatile, and that will certainly affect our tactical approach in races, too,” said Tim Meeusen, Red Bull’s director of development. “But the goal remains the same: to develop our talents and bring them to the WorldTour.”

That means Hincapie is now one step behind the WorldTour squad. Two other Red Bull Rookies also signed pro contracts for 2027, so six out of 13 riders will race pro next season.

Budding superstar Finn also raced on the U19 squad and two years on Red Bull’s Rookies before graduating to the WorldTour in 2027 .

Hincapie will have a few years to race at the U23 level, but those are good odds.

The other big U.S. signing is Klau, who signs with Red Bull’s U19 squad grenke-Auto Eder after racing in 2026 on Hot Tubes, one of the top junior teams in the U.S.

Hot Tubes’ alumni list includes WorldTour stars like Magnus Sheffield, AJ August, Artem Shmidt, and Matteo Jorgenson.

Klau also got a taste of European racing this year with USA Cycling’s junior team, with a top 20 at the Course de la Paix Juniors, before a knee injury kept him out of nationals.

“An injury brought my road season to an early end, which definitely wasn’t part of the plan, but it’s also been a year that’s taught me a lot and given me plenty to take forward,” Klau wrote on Instagram.

Talent recruiters saw enough to make Klau one of six new signings on a 12-rider junior squad for 2027. The team also launched a cyclocross program this winter.

It’s a long way from a junior team to the WorldTour, but being inside Red Bull’s structure will give him a good shot.

The promotions also come after a quiet transfer season for the Red Bull WorldTour team.

After signing Evenepoel for 2026, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe’s only outside transfer for 2027 is Georg Steinhauser from EF Education-EasyPost. The four Rookies getting the bump to the WorldTour squad are Red Bull’s only other 2026-27 market moves.

That makes Klau and Hincapie as the first Americans to be tapped by Red Bull’s cutting-edge development teams.

Like most other major WorldTour operations, Red Bull is betting big on its internal talent program to discover its next generation of stars.

So having two Americans in the pipeline confirms that U.S. prospects are getting noticed by some of Europe’s biggest teams.

Could these two someday races alongside Evenepoel in the WorldTour?

Maybe. At least they’ll start in the pole position.

Teams are floating a new project to collectively sell what they bring to the peloton. (Photo: Loic VENANCE / AFP via Getty Images)

Top pro teams are taking another stab at trying to fix cycling’s business model.

Some 24 squads are forming a company designed to turn their collective commercial muscle into new revenue steams.

Collective Cycling Group Ltd. (CCG), a UK-based business owned by participating teams, announced a shareholder agreement including teams from the men’s and women’s WorldTour and ProTeam ranks.

Discussions with additional teams are ongoing, a statement confirmed Wednesday.

“Teams carry much of the sporting and financial risk in professional cycling, while many of the sport’s commercial opportunities remain fragmented,” CCG director Oliver Ciesla said in the announcement. “The UCI reform process creates a first opportunity to address these challenges together.”

Instead of making a run directly at TV rights, which are controlled by races, teams are looking at what they bring to the table in the form of cycling’s biggest stars.

The idea is to bundle what they have into something bigger that fans, broadcasters, and sponsors might be interested in paying money for.

That includes team commercial rights, data, media content, merchandising, hospitality, and fan experiences.

The end game is to give teams a stronger financial footing rather than leaving them constantly chasing the next sponsor and relying almost exclusively on sponsorship backing to underwrite ever-rising team budgets.

The announcement follows the stalled ONE Cycling project , which died on the vine after the UCI rejected it in June 2025 .

Corporate filings show CCG previously operated under the name OneCycling Limited, according to Reuters .

The release doesn’t mention a new racing series or a call for shared broadcast revenues.

Instead, the focus is on developing commercial opportunities around assets the teams already hold.

They hope to organize their newest project as part of the UCI’s ongoing Project 2030 effort to reshape professional road cycling.

The announcement does not identify the 24 teams, disclose financial commitments, or set a timetable for its first products.

Cycling’s tried this before. Let’s see if something will change.

Roglič joins NSN on a one-year deal. (Photo: Marco BERTORELLO / AFP via Getty Images)

Primož Roglič will race in 2027 and will join NSN Cycling on a one-year deal.

In a late-hour move, the deal means the 37-year-old Slovenian will be in the WorldTour peloton next season.

“I always like challenges,” Roglič said in a team note. “That’s why I’m here, to take these on together and see what the future brings us.

“It took me some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never. It feels like the perfect connection.”

Roglič, one of the superstars over the past decade, was looking down the barrel at possible retirement at the end of 2026.

Talks with several teams ended without a signature , but things came together quickly with NSN Cycling.

“From the first moment we spoke, it was evident that Primož still has a lot of passion for the sport and a drive to be the best he can,” said NSN Cycling general manager Kjell Carlström. “It was an easy decision to make.”

The former ski jumper ended his three-year run with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after a season that included second overall at the Vuelta a España and a win at the European time trial championship.

It was more of a question if he wanted to keep racing and at what price.

Roglič was sometimes bizarrely ambivalent in his public statements about his future, but he was talking with several teams behind the scenes.

Talks petered out, however, with one team after another. NSN offered a one-year contract but no financial details were revealed.

Roglič was reportedly earning around $3 million a year with Red Bull, so a high asking price might have been a factor on some teams taking a pass on the veteran.

Roglič — a winner of five grand tours — will link up with Richard Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt on the reinvigorated NSN lineup.

“This signing reflects the ambition we have for the future. We want to compete at the highest level, challenge for major results and continue building a team capable of achieving great things,” Carlström said. “We are confident that Primož can play an important role in that journey, and we look forward to seeing him race in NSN colors.”

Roglič scored nearly 1,000 UCI points in 2026 , something that will come in handy if he can repeat it next season for NSN Cycling.

The team — formerly Israel-Premier Tech — finished ranked 19th in the rolling three-year WorldTour rankings, one spot out of the guaranteed top 18 licenses.

There’s no news yet on a possible calendar, but at NSN he should see plenty of chances to race.

“I still believe I have some work to do, in both racing and with myself,” Roglič said. “I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things.”

The team broke the news on social media, with a smiling Roglič using a “like and follow” of the team’s social media channel.

Roglič — who was beaten by Tadej Pogačar at the wild TT finale at the 2020 Tour de France — will join his new teammates at a winter camp in Spain next month.

Pogačar hinted that Flanders and Roubaix could be in the cards for 2027. (Photo: Gruber Images)

If anyone is doubting Tadej Pogačar and what his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España might mean for 2027, rest assured.

Don’t worry, Pogi fans, it doesn’t appear that anything will change.

Pogačar sounds as ambitious as ever and said a return to the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix could be in the cards in 2027.

“There is a good chance that I will be at the start again, yes,” he told HLN . “I am already looking forward to it, because they are fun races.”

“Fun” for Pogačar usually means misery for everyone else, but fans absolutely love seeing the world No. 1 race the iconic northern classics .

Pogačar has already singled out the Tour de France , unfinished business at the Vuelta, and a run at a record-tying third worlds in Sallanches as major goals for 2027.

Some wondered if that loaded back-end calendar might mean an easier start to next season, especially since he hasn’t raced since his crash on August 29.

But from what Pogačar told the Belgian outlet Het Laatste Nieuws at the annual padel tournament hosted by his agent Alex Carera in Italy, it doesn’t sound like it.

The quick grab with journalists provided some fresh hints of what next year’s comeback season might look like.

Pogačar admitted the obvious that the 71km of time trial kilometers in the 2027 Tour suits Remco Evenepoel. He also made it clear that he still sees Jonas Vingegaard as a contender on any course.

King Pog doesn’t appear to be losing any sleep over it either, even if some are hyping the 2027 Tour as the “Anti-Pogačar” course .

“I haven’t really looked at the course in detail yet, but there is indeed some time trialing involved,” he said. “That is good for Remco, but as I always say, in the Tour, you can’t hide anywhere. You have to be strong for three weeks in every discipline.

“Whether that’s uphill or on the time trial bike. And you have to be able to maintain focus. That won’t be any different next year.”

The Tour is all but certain to be at the center of his calendar for 2027. After winning the record-tying fifth yellow jersey, he wants to make official history by going for number six.

If he does show up for the Flanders-Roubaix double again, that’s the best indication yet there won’t be any lingering physical impacts from the Vuelta crash.

Roubaix and the Vuelta remain one of the few major races Pogačar has yet to win .

After a few weeks off the bike following surgery in September, Pogačar is back to training after the heavy crash that ended his Vuelta and cut short his 2026 season.

After missing the worlds in Montréal, his UAE teammate Brandon McNulty will be racing in the rainbow jersey , so this season Pogačar won’t be donning the stripes.

“I enjoyed the off-season. The first training sessions didn’t go very smoothly, but things have been going better for the past week,” he said. “My rides are getting longer and I can already pick up the intensity a bit.”

Pogačar’s social media feed has been filled with weddings, trips, coffee rides, sessions in the gym, some jogging, lots of food, and yes, a few longer bike rides.

After two documentaries recently dropped , Pocačar is enjoying his last few days of quiet home life before joining his UAE Emirates-XRG teammates in Spain next month for the team’s first winter camp.

That’s when Pogačar’s official racing calendar will be sketched out.

We’ll see what team boss Mauro Gianetti has to say.

He tapped the brakes on Pogačar’s desire to return to racing for the European championships in Slovenia, and it was a good thing too, because doctors later found other neck fractures from his Vuelta spill .

From the sounds of things, if Pogačar has his way, he won’t be slowing down at all in 2027.

Marlen Reusser says it's time to call the men's race the Tour de France Hommes. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Marlen Reusser says it’s time for cycling to rethink how it brands races by gender.

Instead of having the Tour de France and the Tour de France Femmes , the Swiss star suggests adding “Hommes” to the men’s race, all in the name of fairness.

Speaking on the Domestique Hotseat podcast, the Movistar rider said her frustration peaked at October’s presentation of the 2027 routes in Paris, where Tour director Christian Prudhomme and Tour de France Femmes director Marion Rousse shared the stage.

“The Tour director comes on the stage and introduces the women’s Tour director, Marion Rousse, at his side. You feel like he’s ruling it all, that it’s his Tour, the men’s Tour, and we are guests there,” Reusser told Domestique . “Marion is also allowed to say something, to say hello, but we’re the guests.”

Reusser first raised the subject with Cycling Weekly in October, first saying she thinks “Hommes” should be part of the conversation.

Prudhomme has said the Tour de France is the traditional name for the men’s race, which dates to 1903.

Speaking to Cycling Weekly after last month’s route presentation, he said that “the Tour is the Tour, and we’re absolutely delighted that there’s another race.”

In French, “femmes” translates to women, and “hommes” is men.

Reusser was quick to credit organizers for the growth of the women’s race since its launch in its current form in 2022.

But she also wants that progress to extend to the language surrounding cycling’s races.

“But I wish that very soon it’s not the Tour, it’s the men’s Tour. And we are guests that can have a little Tour also, but it’s the Tour,” she said. “And you can check the dates, from this to this is the women’s, from this to this is the men’s.

“And it doesn’t matter, and it can be just as interesting, just as cool,” she said. “I don’t want to be a decoration of a male sport.”

The issue is becoming a talking point as more races and teams have both men’s and women’s events and squads.

Many of the major teams, like Lidl-Trek and Movistar, do not differentiate between the two genders.

Some races that have both men’s and women’s editions follow the pattern used by ASO. Other examples are the Giro d’Italia and Giro d’Italia Women or the Vuelta a España and La Vuelta Femenina.

Reusser told Domestique that tradition shouldn’t prevent change.

“Let’s say the UCI decided there is a rule that you cannot put ‘women’ or ‘femmes’ in the name of a race when you don’t have the same in the name of the men’s race. Then you could not say it’s tradition,” she said. “You would just have to change it, and I think it would go fast. It’s a matter of how much people really want to change stuff.”

Right now, there are no official UCI rules outlining how race organizers name their events.

Reusser — who cited her background in medicine — said words help establish the hierarchy.

“If we word things as standard men, we think standard men,” she said. “So if we want to have it different, we need to start wording things different.”

Should the men's Tour de France also be called 'Hommes'? (Photo: Gruber Images)

There’s the Tour de France and the Tour de France Femmes . Should the men’s race carry “Hommes” for equal billing?

The Swiss star wants “Hommes” added to the men’s Tour if the women’s edition carries “Femmes,” arguing that cycling’s language still treats men as the default and women as the supporting act.

“I don’t want to be a decoration of a male sport,” she told the Domestique Hotseat podcast.

That question is timely as more races hold both men’s and women’s editions.

What’s the best way to name paired events?

Is adding one word a step toward equal billing? Or should the Tour keep its historic name?

Reusser also floated another idea of having the UCI require matching names across men’s and women’s events.

ASO , meanwhile, seems reluctant to change its brand name after more than 100 years of history in the men’s race.

There is a giant vault in Bolzano, Italy that can simulate elevation higher than Mount Everest, a freeze as cold as Siberia, and temperatures so hot that they are used to help train firefighters. On October 21, I stepped into that vault wearing nothing but a cycling kit and shoes.

As I swung my leg over a stationary bike, the fans revved up in front of me as the chamber adjusted its climate to match Stage 2 of this year’s Tour de France. It was a hot day in Barcelona when Isaac del Toro won ahead of Tadej Pogacar and Remco Evenepoel. By the end of the Tour, it was the hottest race on record with an average temperature of 32.4°C (90.3°F) across the 21 stages.

Excessive heat usually means a decline in performance. But with the advent of heat training, cooling strategies, and ever-improving clothing technology, professional cyclists are faster than ever, even during the hottest Tour de France in history.

The moment I stepped into the vault — the TerraX Cube — I knew what was at stake. I was here alongside the CORE team and more than 20 other journalists to test the new Q36.5 Gregarius Pro Evo Jersey, Base Layer Subzero, and Dottore Pro Bib Shorts. The vault was set to 35°C (95°F) degrees with a humidity of 50%, far from the ideal temperature to achieve peak performance. I had just done a heat training session in CORE’s Sweatlab, so I had a baseline of data for what I could expect as my core temperature rose.

Not only were we going to ride in excessive heat, we were going to simulate the finale of Stage 2 of the Tour using a custom workout on Zwift. Here was the workout , along with my power targets based on my FTP:

I was already dripping sweat during the warmup thanks to the ambient temperature, and my sweat rate intensified as my power increased to 360w. After a quick recovery, we began the hardest part of the test (in my opinion): four minutes at VO2 Max in 95-degree heat. This is the type of effort short enough that you can maintain an output above threshold, but long enough that your heart rate and RPE will be jacked up by the end of the effort.

The final few intervals went by fast as I could see the metaphorical finish line in front of me. And just like that, it was all over. CORE gathered data from our body temperature sensors, and we shuffled our way into the cool hallway. The testing was over; now it was time to look at the results.

To my surprise, our performances in the heat chamber didn’t drop off significantly. In fact, many riders (myself included) performed at their best despite the hot conditions. This was a sharp contrast to my data from CORE’s Sweatlab where I pushed myself to the limit without ever breaking 300w.

The lab test at CORE – done two days before the test in Bolzano – was a data-gathering mission. I wasn’t there to chase power PBs or set an impressive time. I was there to sweat; and that I did.

During the normal cooling conditions, I wore a cycling kit and had two fans pointed towards me. I was riding on a Zwift Ride with ERG mode turned on, so my power output was steady to the Watt. The initial 15-minute interval established the baseline where my heart rate was steady at 138 bpm, and my core temperature stabilized at 38°C (100.4°F).

The hard part was up next: 35 minutes of heat training. That meant pulling on the CORE heat training suit, turning the fans off, and turning the heater on. Within minutes, my sweat started pooling on the floor. Over the course of 35 minutes, my heart rate rose from 138 bpm to 175 bpm without any change in power. I rode at 280w the entire time, but it felt like I was doing a threshold interval for the last 15 minutes.

That is the damage that heat can do to your performance. Without sufficient cooling, Zone 2 power can feel like Zone 4 power once your heat strain reaches a certain level. That was the kind of performance degradation that CORE was looking for in the Italian climate cube. But the closer they looked at the results, the more they realized that the clothing had worked.

We were all wearing Q36.5 kit in the climate chamber, specifically designed for use in 30°C+ (86°F) heat. Tom Pidcock loves heat training, and it was no surprise to hear that he plays a major role in the R&D of Q36.5 kit. (Fun fact: he’s also the only rider on Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team who wears an XXS skinsuit.)

As I pored through my own performance data, I remembered how good my legs felt during the final two-minute interval in the heat chamber. Despite feeling hot, my body had performed extremely well in the conditions. Personally, that is the biggest difference that I’ve noticed after doing a heat training block.

Without heat acclimatization, my body has typically reacted to the heat like it did in CORE’s Sweatlab. My heart rate would rise uncontrollably as my legs are drained of their strength. But after a big heat training block, I noticed that I could still hit my best power numbers in excessively hot conditions. Not only would my heart rate be 10 bpm lower than expected, but it would stabilize during long efforts in the heat – quite the opposite of what I experienced in the CORE Sweatlab.

One of my biggest takeaways was that the clothing had worked. This wasn’t the only heat adaptation method that I asked Q36.5 and CORE about during this trip. I also asked about cold drinks, pouring water over your head, rubbing ice cubes on your wrists, and of course, heat training. Let’s start with what does work.

Cold drinks and gels are probably the most effective ways to cool your body from the inside out. When you’re talking about performance degradation in the heat, you are most often talking about an increase in core temperature as well as an increase in skin temperature. This is known as heat strain, something that CORE quantifies with their sensor and app, and the key metric that many riders use for heat training.…

This week, Amflow is expanding beyond electric mountain bikes with the launch of its first city commuter line, the Amflow UE Series. On the surface, it sounds like yet another unfamiliar name offering a high-powered commuter bike, but the news is a bit bigger than that. What this really means is that DJI-backed Amflow and its Avinox motor are making the jump from e-MTB to city riding.

Available now in the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro builds, the platform pairs that drive system with a claimed 2.35-kilogram full-carbon, low step-through frame to hit a complete bike weight of 20.9 kilograms, or roughly 46 pounds. It makes for an impressive offering on paper and raises the obvious question of whether putting that kind of hardware into a transportation-focused package will reshape the commuter market the same way Amflow did e-MTB.

Rather than offering a traditional multi-size run at launch, Amflow designed the standard UE frame to accommodate riders between 5 feet, 1 inch and 6 feet, 3 inches using two interchangeable stem heights. A dedicated small frame for riders between 4 feet, 7 inches and 5 feet, 3 inches is scheduled to arrive in 2027.

Beyond that, the bike follows expected commuter design patterns, leaning toward comfort and visibility. The first lever of that focus is frame geometry, starting with a step-through frame and flat handlebars to put the rider in an upright position. That layout is paired with 65 mm of front suspension, a seatpost with 125 mm of height adjustment and 30 mm of suspension travel, and wide 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires. Braking comes from Magura 180 mm disc brakes with three-finger levers. For hauling cargo, Amflow equips the bike with a front rack rated for 20 kilograms (about 44 pounds) and a rear MIK HD-compatible rack rated for 27 kilograms (about 59.5 pounds).

The biggest news here is that the motor that disrupted the e-MTB market is expanding into new territory. Powering both builds is the Avinox M2 drive unit, which Amflow claims delivers up to 125 Nm of torque and an 8-to-1 maximum assist ratio. According to the brand, the motor can climb 30% grades under load while keeping operating noise below 45 dBA. The system also includes a traction control feature and a new Auto Boost mode that automatically increases power output on steep hills or loaded starts without rider input.

Both builds use a removable 600Wh battery, with Amflow claiming a maximum range of 132 kilometers (about 82 miles) under controlled testing conditions. It charges from zero to 100% in 2 hours and 23 minutes, and riders can set a custom charge limit to preserve cell longevity.

Both models also feature electronic shifting with automatic and smooth-shifting modes, leaving the drivetrain as the main mechanical difference between the two. The UE Carbon Pro uses a custom three-speed electronic internal geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt, which allows riders to shift while stopped and avoids chain maintenance or greasy clothes — though it costs more. Alternatively, the less expensive Amflow UE Carbon uses a 10-speed electronic rear derailleur co-developed with TRP.

Amflow leans heavily into its connected ecosystem on the UE Series, integrating several new Avinox accessories directly into the bike. Control centers on a 1.4-inch DP200 handlebar touchscreen paired with a rotating phone mount that offers 15W wireless and 20W USB-C charging. The integrated lighting system features automatic dusk activation, high- and low-beam switching and a brake-sensing rear light.

Through the Avinox Ride app, riders can pair multiple bikes to one account, merge ride files, sync with an Apple Watch and control compatible DJI Osmo cameras from the handlebar. The system can also pair with a heart rate monitor to adjust motor assist automatically based on a target heart rate zone.

On the security front, a single key operates both the battery lock and an integrated 10 mm hardened steel ART 2-Star horseshoe lock. The bike also supports Apple Find My tracking and an app-based Lost Mode designed to disable the bike remotely if it is stolen.

Both the Amflow UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro are available immediately through Amflow’s website and authorized dealers. U.S. pricing is $3,499 for the UE Carbon and $3,899 for the UE Carbon Pro.

Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.
