Verstappen did not run until late in the session but was complaining about a problem with his engine.

Perhaps surprisingly given the conditions, the session was incident-free, although it was stopped briefly in the closing stages to recover a plastic bag that had blown on to the circuit.

Williams driver Alex Albon said: "I'm always surprised when I see no crashes. Trickiest track of the year, lowest grip of the year, these cars and a wet track is a lot of sliding."

The forecast is for dry weather for the rest of the weekend and the teams' focus will be on understanding the tyres, with warm-up so difficult in the cold conditions and with low loads going through the tyres.

This issue is exacerbated this year with the new 'straight-line mode', in which the wings open to reduce drag on the straights to aid energy recovery.

Russell said: "It's always a challenge here in Vegas but the added challenge this year with the nature of the cars, the SM zones everywhere, you're not putting any vertical load in the tyres so they are getting substantially cooler in the straight than in the previous years and they were already pretty cool."

In the first practice session, no driver completed a timed lap because the track was extremely wet and teams preferred to save their limited allocation of wet-weather tyres.

Hamilton said: "It wasn't a great day just sitting around waiting. You can't really test much in those conditions. And everything you learn from today you have to forget because tomorrow is supposed to be dry, so we kind of start from tomorrow.

"Everyone is (going in blind). No-one has put the slicks on, so we will have to react quickly. Hopefully, it's not bad and we are there or thereabouts."

Piastri will have a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine-part allowance this season.

The new internal combustion engine the Australian needs as a result of a failure at the Mexico City Grand Prix two races ago is his fifth of the season - only four are permitted.

Piastri and team-mate Norris will also use the latest turbo Mercedes have produced under F1's engine upgrade scheme but that comes penalty-free.

That is not the case for Williams' Carlos Sainz, who will take the new turbo but it is his fifth of the season, so he also has a 10-place penalty which team-mate Alex Albon avoids despite also fitting the new turbo.

At the factory team, only Antonelli will use the new turbo. The team decided it was not worth Russell having it as it would have given him a 15-place grid penalty.

The turbo provides only a small performance upgrade and is more aimed at expanding the engine's useability for the 2027 season.

Bearman also has a grid penalty for engine changes and is set to start from the back of the grid.

Is Ollie Bearman's career in danger of stalling by being at Haas and stuck in the Ferrari bottleneck? He obviously has the talent to be a world championship contender but being stuck at the back of the grid can't be doing his career any good. - Dave

Oliver Bearman has still not been confirmed as a Haas driver for 2027, even though both parties say that's what they want.

From Bearman's point of view, it's not hard to see why he might be asking a few questions about his future.

He is a member of the Ferrari driver academy and they show no sign of wanting him not to be, but at the same time they are not showing much sign of wanting to promote him to the senior team.

In that sense, Bearman's future hangs to a degree on Lewis Hamilton's.

Hamilton is talking about staying in F1 at least until 2030, which would mean a new contract at the end of next year, presumably with Ferrari.

But will Ferrari keep him? That is unknown, amid what has undoubtedly been some tension between him, team-mate Charles Leclerc and the team management this season.

If Hamilton stays, Bearman would be within his rights to ask how they see his future, and to ask for the chance to look for opportunities elsewhere.

How secure is James Vowles' position at Williams? He seems like a great guy, always very open and honest. But the fact remains that the team targeted this year for a big performance jump and they've actually gone backwards. Is Vowles running out of time? - James

Williams have had a bad season in 2026. There is no question about that.

For three years since Vowles became team principal in 2023, he had been talking about 2026 as the team's opportunity to take a significant step towards their ambitions of returning to the front.

Having finished fifth in 2025 - a result that even surprised the team - another step forward was expected this year under the new rules.

But that's not what happened. Instead, Williams have gone significantly backwards.

The car was late, too heavy and lacked downforce. Little relative progress has been made through the year and they lie ninth in the constructors' championship with three races to go and will almost certainly finish there.

All year, Vowles has been explaining that the new rules exposed pressure points in the Williams factory that he had not realised existed. Essentially, the factory systems were not able to cope with the demands being put on them.

He says they needed this experience to be able to fix them and move forwards to a better place.

A critic might question why Vowles had not realised they were there in the three years he had been leading the time up to that point.

Drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon have been unimpressed by what has happened this year.

But Vowles succeeded in getting both to stay on for at least one more season. Although whether that was because they retain belief in the team or because they did not have that many better options is a debatable point.

Asked what gave him the confidence to stay, Albon said: "This year I've been brought into a more deeper analysis of where it went wrong from last year to this year.

"So why were we late? Why was the car overweight? What were the reasons? Why did we miss the trick on even the philosophy of the car, for example?

"I'm satisfied with what those reasons are. As simple as that, really.

"At the same time, I also want to see these things materialise and I want to see these changes happen next year."

Albon admitted to there being a "deep frustration shared with the whole team that after all the efforts of prioritising this year's car, we haven't delivered a good job".

A new, lighter chassis was introduced at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. That will be carried over into next year so, as Albon puts it, "we start next year's car with a chassis that's not heavy, that's on the right foot, that we can then start focusing a lot more on not losing weight and a lot more time on aerodynamics and making the car go faster".

Through this season, Vowles has taken to publicly calling for a revision to the cost-cap rules, saying they bake in an advantage for the big teams, and wanting allowances for extra spending for others to catch up.

His critics say that those allowances are already there in one form, and that Vowles is using this as a distraction technique.

Whether his job is on the line if there is not a significant step forward for 2027 after all this is not clear. But the pressure is mounting, and he will certainly have a lot of explaining to do if there isn't.

With Max Verstappen established at Red Bull for the foreseeable future, what is Racing Bulls' real purpose: to discover Max MkII for Red Bull or simply provide a route to finding a reliable number two? Is it time Racing Bulls was allowed to operate as a genuinely independent, competitive team, rather than effectively functioning as Red Bull's driver development programme? - Michael

Racing Bulls' raison d'etre is the same as it has always been through all its name changes since Red Bull bought Minardi at the end of 2005.

That is to act as a training ground for drivers for the main Red Bull team.

It can be argued that the Red Bull young driver programme has not been especially successful.

In 20 years, the only top-line driver it has brought up through the junior categories all the way to being a success at Red Bull Racing was Daniel Ricciardo.

Sebastian Vettel was a BMW driver before Red Bull signed him, and Max Verstappen was plucked straight into F1 by Red Bull after winning a tug-of-war with Mercedes while he was in F3.…

Kimi Antonelli has made history by becoming the youngest title winner in the 77th year of the Formula 1 World Championship.

The Italian, at 20 years and 68 days, has beaten the record of Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 years and 134 days old when he won the first of his four drivers' championships in 2010.

Antonelli, who was still a teenager until 25 August, has secured the title in his second season in the sport.

We take a look at F1's other young champions and how Antonelli's achievement compares with theirs.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season

F1 debut: 2025 Australian Grand Prix (aged 18)

Antonelli has already broken a number of records on the way to becoming F1's youngest champion.

In his second season, he became the youngest driver to achieve a pole position in China and the youngest to lead the championship at the next race in Japan.

In Monaco, he became the youngest driver to complete a 'grand slam' of pole position, fastest lap, leading every lap and winning the race.

All this after a rookie season in 2025 in which there were occasional highs but plenty of errors, and his final total of 150 points was less than half of the 319 accumulated by Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Third full season

Vettel was one of four drivers who could win the title going into the season-ending 2010 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

He was far from the best placed, though, trailing Ferrari's Fernando Alonso by 15 points before the race and his Red Bull team-mate Mark Webber by seven.

The German did what he had to do by winning the grand prix and Alonso could only finish seventh, having become stuck behind the Renault of Vitaly Petrov.

With Webber in eighth, Vettel won the championship by four points from Alonso.

It was yet another F1 record for Vettel. He had become the youngest F1 points scorer on his debut for BMW Sauber in Indianapolis in 2007, before becoming the then youngest pole sitter and race winner at the 2008 Italian Grand Prix for Toro Rosso.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season

F1 debut: 2007 Australian Grand Prix (aged 22)

Lewis Hamilton's debut season in 2007 almost delivered a fairytale title but he faltered in the final two races of the year.

He failed to score in China and finished seventh in Brazil, which allowed Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen to pip both Hamilton and fellow McLaren driver Fernando Alonso by a single point.

Somehow the climax to the 2008 championship, also in Brazil, was even more dramatic.

Hamilton was battling for the title with Ferrari's home favourite Felipe Massa and the Briton's fourth place was going to be enough to secure the crown when a late rain shower changed everything.

Leader Massa and Hamilton were among those who changed to intermediate tyres but Toyota's Timo Glock stayed out, which lifted him up to fourth.

Hamilton, now in fifth, had Toro Rosso's Vettel right behind him and couldn't afford to lose another position. With just over two laps to go, he ran wide and Vettel was through.

Massa crossed the line to win the race with Hamilton still sixth. The Ferrari pit crew, Massa's family and the Brazilian fans celebrated but with the rain intensifying, Glock was slowing on his dry-weather tyres and Hamilton passed him into the final corner to take the title by a single point. It was heart-stopping stuff.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Fourth full season

F1 debut: 2001 Australian Grand Prix (aged 19)

Alonso established control of the 2005 championship early in the season by winning four of the first seven races and never relinquished it.

The Spaniard's speed and consistency ensured he prevailed over Raikkonen, whose McLaren-Mercedes was fast but fragile. A third place at the Brazilian Grand Prix was enough to give Alonso the title with two races to spare.

He won a second consecutive title in 2006, also for Renault, and the 45-year-old remains one of the great personalities and outstanding talents in F1.

He'll be back for another season with Aston Martin in 2027, 26 years after his debut for Minardi.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Seventh full season

F1 debut: 2015 Australian Grand Prix (aged 17)

Hamilton won the title on the final lap of the 2008 season but he would lose it on the final lap in 2021 in circumstances that remain a source of huge controversy.

His rival in a thrilling and intense season-long duel was Red Bull's Max Verstappen. There were plenty of flashpoints along the way and it all came to a climax in Abu Dhabi.

Verstappen and Hamilton went into the final race of the season level on points. The Dutchman qualified on pole but Mercedes' Hamilton beat him off the line and largely controlled the race thereafter, until Williams' Nicholas Latifi crashed with five laps to go, bringing out a safety car.

Hamilton did not have enough of an advantage over second-placed Verstappen to pit for fresh tyres and maintain the lead, so stayed out. Verstappen, with nothing to lose, came in and fitted softs.

Race director Michael Masi allowed the lapped cars between Hamilton and Verstappen to go past, but not those behind the Red Bull. He allowed the race to restart for one final racing lap and Verstappen overtook Hamilton, who was a sitting duck on his old hard tyres.

Verstappen and Hamilton, in their own ways, were both stunned and Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff shouted over the radio to Masi: "No, Michael, no! That was so not right!"

As happened with Vettel from 2010-13, this was the first of four consecutive titles for a Red Bull driver with Verstappen dominating the 2022, 2023 and 2024 seasons.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season

F1 debut: 1970 British Grand Prix (aged 23)

Emerson Fittipaldi became the first Brazilian driver to win the F1 world title in 1972, with five wins from 12 races enough for the Lotus driver to get the better of Jackie Stewart.…

As soft, instrumental opera music plays in the background of a precise temperature-controlled room in northern Italy, Thomaso is using a children's toy ball and hairdryer to perform his meticulous work.

Hugely focused, in a crisp white coat, he moulds a precious sticky black material over and over again for up to six hours.

One day, his fastidiousness may save the life of one of the best athletes in the world.

The room Thomaso works in is called "the magic shop". Its motto? 'One man, one shell.'

Much of what happens inside is top secret. What we can say is the black material Thomaso is working with is a blend of carbon fibre that has to be stored at exactly -16°C. He moulds it into a secret form, layer by layer, after which the entire unit is baked in a vacuum bag at a set pressure at 120C for three-and-a-half hours.

The handmade products he is working on are personally chosen by their clients - for their safety features, as well as comfort, practicality and look.

Thomaso's colleague Sven travels the world between February and December to keep those clients happy. A different country almost every week, with a reliable weather forecast almost as important as a large allowance of hand luggage.

Together with 32 colleagues, Thomaso and Sven work for one of the four leading manufacturers of F1 helmets.

They produce sophisticated engineering masterpieces, and works of art.

"Our philosophy is to make the best product for the best drivers," says chief executive Alberto Dall'Oglio.

In the early days of grand prix racing, protection was rudimentary. Drivers often wore little more than leather flying caps, goggles and - eventually - relatively basic open-face helmets.

Safety standards were inconsistent, materials primitive and the consequences of an accident frequently devastating.

According to the official F1 website, Giuseppe Farina - the first winner of an F1 race and first world champion - competed wearing nothing more than "his trusty cloth cap, two pairs of goggles (he wore the spare pair round his neck), cotton dungarees, leather boots and leather gloves".

The arrival of the full-face helmet in the late 1960s marked a defining moment. Bell introduced its pioneering Star model in 1966, and Dan Gurney became the first driver to race in a full-face helmet in 1968. The face - previously exposed to flying debris, fire and impact - finally had meaningful protection.

Progress was painfully slow, and motorsport's darkest moments repeatedly exposed the limitations of the technology.

In 1976, Niki Lauda 's Ferrari erupted into flames at the Nurburgring. His helmet came loose, leaving his head exposed to the fire. He survived, but suffered severe burns and lifelong injuries. The accident became a defining lesson in the importance of helmet retention, fire resistance and the protection of the driver's entire head.

The tragic deaths of Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna at Imola in 1994, followed by Jules Bianchi's fatal accident at Suzuka in 2014, demonstrated even increasingly sophisticated helmets could not eliminate every danger.

Ratzenberger suffered a fatal basilar skull fracture; Senna succumbed to multiple fractures of the skull base, after a strut from the suspension pierced his helmet.

Bianchi's accident exposed the vulnerability of drivers' heads to heavy external impacts. Helmets are only one part of a much wider safety system, which now includes stronger survival cells, the Hans device and the halo.

In 2004, the FIA introduced its new helmet safety standard, requiring advanced carbon-fibre construction to deliver greater strength, improved impact protection and reduced weight for F1 drivers.

At Bahrain's Sakhir circuit in 2020, Romain Grosjean's Haas split apart against the barriers and burst into flames. After 28 seconds trapped in the wreckage, he emerged with burns to his hands and ankles. His Bell helmet, fire-resistant equipment and the halo were instrumental in saving his life - a powerful testament to decades of safety innovation and engineering.

"Today's helmets are withstanding up to 30 seconds at 700, even 800, degrees," says Dall'Oglio. "Then they have to self-extinguish within 15 seconds."

Dall'Oglio is the CEO of Schuberth Performance, Thomaso an engineer and Sven a racing service technician, working trackside at more than 400 grands prix, preparing helmets and visors for rain, sun or floodlights.

Needing to avoid any impact on the helmets, he must carry them - sometimes five or six at a time - to races.

Schuberth, a German firm, has a long history in head protection. Founded in 1922, the company began making industrial products before moving into helmet linings in the late 1920s, then mining and motorcycle helmets in the 1950s.

With its HQ in Magdeburg and F1 helmet production in Schio, northern Italy, it produces special helmets for military forces - made of Kevlar, and some of a similar carbon - in the same factory as the F1 helmets.

Its motorsport credentials grew considerably around the turn of the millennium.

Following Michael Schumacher's British Grand Prix accident in 1999, Schuberth developed a new generation of racing helmets, subsequently worn by Schumacher and other leading drivers.

Of the current drivers, four-time world champion Max Verstappen is the most prominent to wear a Schuberth helmet. He is joined by Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar, Cadillac's Sergio Perez, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls.

Dall'Oglio's team hand-makes about 250 helmets a year.

An F1 helmet is a remarkable marriage of science and aesthetics.

Constructed using advanced composite materials, including carbon fibre, it must be exceptionally strong while remaining light enough to minimise strain on a driver's neck.

Visors, ventilation systems, fire-resistant linings, communication equipment, a straw-like drinks system and carefully designed retention mechanisms all contribute to its performance.…

Lando Norris says qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix brought "some of the wettest conditions" in which he had ever driven - and he is hoping for more rain in the race on Sunday.

It was the third consecutive year in which Norris has taken pole in Brazil, and it came in a session that was stopped for nearly an hour and a half because conditions were too dangerous to continue when officials initially tried to start it.

Many drivers agreed that conditions were borderline in the extreme.

Mercedes driver George Russell, who qualified second to Norris and was miffed about a team miscommunication that he felt robbed him of pole, said: "Q1 was extremely challenging. The visibility was zero down the straight into Turn Four. I was wheel-spinning in fifth gear, over 200km/h (120mph), aquaplaning.

"When you're aquaplaning on the straight and you can't see in front of you, it's... I'm not even sure what the word is to describe it.

"It does seem a bit crazy. I guess that's what we have to deal with.

"I love driving in the rain. I love driving in the rain here, but at some point, if that was a race, there was no way we should be driving in that because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident are very, very high."

The rain - combined with grid penalties for four of the usual front-runners, including Russell - has produced an unfamiliar grid with several drivers exploiting the opportunity of the weather to produce their best results of the year.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson - who still does not know whether he has a seat next year - and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg occupy the second row.

Haas driver Oliver Bearman is sixth, and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso and Williams' Alex Albon in eighth and ninth both made it into the top 10 for the first time in 2026.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who won this race in the wet two years ago from 17th on the grid, start 20th and 21st after replacing their engines and exceeding their allowance for the year.

Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc, who qualified fourth, has a 10-place penalty, also for engine usage.

Sunday's forecast is for light rain, and the unpredictability of the weather at the Interlagos track, which is famous for it, means the teams and drivers will be open-minded about what to expect.

Norris takes pole in rain-delayed qualifying

Hamilton & Verstappen to start from back in Brazil

Norris had not taken pole since the Spanish Grand Prix in September, and although his McLaren has upgrades on it, which he acknowledged had improved the car, he felt he owed it to the conditions.

"We're lucky it's wet, because if it was dry, I wouldn't be sitting here," said Norris. "In the dry, we definitely didn't have the pace.

"We've looked better this weekend but we still had some small issues, and we've not been up to the pace of the Mercedes. The wet kind of gave me an opportunity and I made the most of it.

"I'm hoping for a wet race. There's a good likelihood it'll be wet. There's a bit of rain, I think, tomorrow at times, and it'll still be damp through the day, so we could just have an exciting race with a little bit of everything, honestly.

"These are conditions where you feel like you can make a little bit more of a difference at times, for sure. And I feel like I'm against good guys who also have the capabilities of going for pole, and today we managed to do it because I put two good laps together and I had a good gap, and we managed things well.

"It was tense when you want to push so much. You need to kind of learn about the conditions, but you also need to not make a single mistake.

"But actually, I felt pretty confident through the whole of qualifying. Q3 was definitely the trickiest because it was also difficult to see, because of the light, where were the dry bits, the wet bits and puddles, things like that. So, more rewarding."

For Russell, there was another disappointment in a season that has been full of them.

Last weekend, he had to watch team-mate Kimi Antonelli clinch the world title and become the youngest champion in history.

Here, he felt pole was his had he not been told to back off on what he felt would have been his fastest lap after he came across Albon in the twisty middle sector.

The team felt the imminent heavier rain would hold off long enough for him to do another lap. They were wrong, and Russell swore over the radio asking what had happened.

He was reminded by team boss Toto Wolff that he was still P2, to which he responded, short-tempered, that he was not there to be second.

It might have seemed a loss of perspective, given his five-place grid penalty meant he would not have been on pole even if he had been fastest.

But for Russell his feelings were rooted in self-validation after a difficult year, and it was not related to the fact that it promoted Antonelli to second.

"Gives me the confidence and reminds me again that I haven't forgotten how to drive," he said. "That's important in circumstances like these and it would have meant a lot to me to clinch the pole with a great performance like we showed in qualifying."

He added: "I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace, along with Lando's, was by far the best out there.

"In the rain here, it's always a challenge. I hope it is wet tomorrow. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet."

The wet conditions provided Alonso with a chance to demonstrate the waste of talent that this year's uncompetitive Aston Martin-Honda car has created.

With its down-on-power and difficult engine, Alonso has been struggling all year. There have been few chinks of light.

This was a rare opportunity to shine, and he took it.

Up at the sharp end throughout, he dropped away - if only relatively - in the final session when he could not get temperature in his tyres. It may have been because he was first in the queue in the pit lane in his eagerness to get in a lap time before the rain worsened again.…

McLaren's Lando Norris converted pole position into a race win at a wet-dry-wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.

Max Verstappen came through the field to take second after starting at the back of the grid because of an engine penalty, while his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar was on the podium in third.

Mercedes sealed the constructors' championship for the first time since 2021 at Interlagos following a fourth-place finish for George Russell and fifth for new world champion Kimi Antonelli.

Here BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Lewis Hamilton has just completed his 400th F1 grand prix, with more than 100 of these races having him on pole position. There are drivers with a better pole percentage than this, so just how good is he and for how much longer can he stay at the top? - Clive

Lewis Hamilton is unquestionably one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers in history.

He's statistically the most successful - with the most race wins and pole positions.

He's tied with Michael Schumacher for the most championships with seven, and many would - and do - argue he should have eight, given the controversy of the mishandled final race of the 2021 season.

Greatness as an F1 driver is about more than raw statistics, but even so Hamilton has consistently proved to be at the very highest level, with a series of outstanding drives in races that will go down in history as some of the greatest ever.

Examples of those would be the 2008 British Grand Prix and the 2021 Brazilian Grand Prix, along with many others.

He's also won races in nearly all his seasons - the only exceptions being 2022, 2023 and 2025.

There is no question that, within the context of his remarkable career, Hamilton struggled relatively in the era of 'ground-effect' cars from 2022-25.

He was beaten by Mercedes team-mate George Russell in two of their three seasons together, and looked a shadow of his usual self against Charles Leclerc in 2025.

Those performances led some to question why a driver formerly famed and lauded for his adaptability did not seem as able to adapt to the driving style required of those cars.

And that, in turn, led to questions as to whether the fact he apparently could not was related to his age - he is now 41.

But with this year's cars, Hamilton is back in much more familiar territory, is performing extremely well again and is neck-and-neck with Leclerc.

Those questions about the four years from 2022-25 will remain just that, but there is no doubt Hamilton is sensitive to them. He has referenced them a number of times this year, including last weekend in Brazil, when the topic of his 400th race came up.

"I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," he said. "It's crazy because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week, I still have the pace, I still have the speed and I still have the dedication, which is most important and the focus. For me, that number is kind of irrelevant."

Longevity in sport depends on many factors, and each athlete is different.

On the face of it, however, there is no obvious reason why, on an age front, Hamilton cannot continue for a good few more years - Fernando Alonso is 45 and is still performing at an extremely high level, as he proved yet again in Brazil at the weekend.

Hamilton has said he wants to race at least until F1 returns to Africa, which will not be until 2030 at the earliest, when he, too, will be 45.

For that, he will need at least one new contract, as his current one with Ferrari is believed to end next year.

We heard, and saw, a lot of 'yo-yo racing' in the first half of the season. This seems to have reduced. What has changed? - Ali

'Yo-yo racing' was a term coined at the start of this year for a new character of on-track battle in which cars swapped positions multiple times over a series of laps.

This was caused by the new power-units introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power and are fundamentally energy starved.

The operations of these engines included 'overtake' and 'boost' modes.

'Boost' is a facility for a driver to demand extra electrical energy whenever he wants, as long as the battery has charge.

'Overtake' mode gives a driver following within one second of a car in front an extra 0.5MJ of energy recovery and deployment capability per lap.

At the start of the season, this - combined with the teams' and drivers' relative unfamiliarity with the new technology - led to a number of examples of yo-yo racing in the early grands prix.

This is where one driver has more electrical energy available, uses it to overtake, whereupon the driver behind now has more and overtakes back, and so on.

This has been less prevalent recently and there are two reasons for that.

Primarily, the tracks in recent weeks have been less 'energy-starved'. And the more energy-starved a car is at a track, the more likelihood there is for yo-yo racing.

The overtaking comes from the variation in energy levels, and being at tracks where drivers can't use all the energy they want all the time.

On top of that, drivers and teams have now been using the engines for a season and are much more on top of how to use them, and therefore how not to leave themselves vulnerable.

At the same time, rule changes have been introduced since the start of the season to reduce the impact of energy starvation, such as imposing energy limits on tracks where it is a major issue. This flattens out the peaks and troughs in energy availability.

And into next year and beyond further steps are being taken to make the engines more "normal" in operation - by changing the energy split to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.…

Valtteri Bottas has been retained by Cadillac for the 2027 Formula 1 season.

The future of the 37-year-old Finn had been in doubt as the American team endure a difficult maiden campaign.

To date, they have failed to collect a point in either the drivers' or constructors' championship.

However, two-time championship runner-up Bottas will race again with them next year.

"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027," said Bottas, who is preparing for Sunday's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

"We knew building a new Formula One team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come. I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."

The news follows the recent announcement that Mexican Sergio Perez, 36, will also be remaining with Cadillac until 2029 after signing a contract extension.

Cadillac had been considering whether to promote their American reserve driver, Colton Herta, into Bottas' seat.

The 26-year-old former Indycar driver has earned enough points to apply for the superlicence required to drive in F1 through his outings in practice this year.

But the feeling was that there was no obvious upgrade to Bottas and that the Finn had not been given a fair run in what has been a difficult debut season for Cadillac beset by reliability problems and lack of pace.

The team decided that they needed stability for their second season, and that the experience provided by Perez and Bottas, who have both won grands prix, was as important as ever.

Herta had given up his seat in Indycar to drive in Formula 2 this season with the idea of preparing himself for F1.

However, he has had a difficult season and lies 19th in the championship with two races remaining.

Herta now faces a decision as to what to do in 2027.

Cadillac are still open to the idea of him graduating to F1, perhaps in 2028, but it is not clear where he may race next year while he waits to see whether that opportunity arises.

TWG, the US consortium which runs Cadillac, has other teams in other categories for which Herta could race alongside any F1 reserve role that might be on offer.

One of the options would involve a return to Indycar, or Herta could perhaps move into endurance racing.

Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty will hand pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Antonelli, running at the back of the pack of cars in qualifying and maximising his tow, beat Verstappen by 0.258 seconds.

But the new world champion has a five-place grid penalty for using more than permitted number of engine components and will start sixth.

The Italian's team-mate George Russell was just 0.073secs behind Verstappen and will start alongside the Dutchman on the front row.

McLaren's Lando Norris qualified fourth, and will start third, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

Both Ferraris were eliminated in the second session and qualified 11th and 12th with Charles Leclerc ahead of Lewis Hamilton.

Each will be promoted a place by a 10-place penalty for McLaren's Oscar Piastri, who qualified seventh.

Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad, sixth fastest, is the last driver to be promoted as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh with Alpine's Pierre Gasly eighth and Franco Colapinto ninth.

Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar

Antonelli's final run did not start auspiciously as he and Russell became tangled up with the Alpines and Racing Bulls as they sought the best track position to optimise the slipstream effect.

Antonelli ended up the last driver to run and made it to the line with only one second to spare before the chequered flag, one second behind Lindblad.

Normally, being so close to the car in front would be a compromise but in Las Vegas it magnified the tow effect and Antonelli leapt to the front. "That was all the tow," he said over the radio after being told he was on pole.

"Starting the lap, I was only one second behind the car in front and I thought I was screwed," he said. "But the tow is so powerful here."

Verstappen, who has won two of the three Las Vegas Grands Prix, said: "I have been struggling with some weird issues that were also in the car in Brazil and just trying to get my head around how to deal with that.

"In qualifying we managed to make it work. Had a solid qualifying. My first lap in qualifying was pretty much as good as it could be with the tow, so to be on the front row is good for us.

"It was solid in the corners, and you have a bit of dirty air, but it is insane how much you gain on the straights."

Russell had looked in the running for the pole, but was happy with his session despite missing out.

"Overall it's been a very solid session and a solid day," he said.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance than in Mexico when I was on the front row.

"Kimi did a great job and he probably thought it wasn't going to work out so well being so close but with the tow it worked out."

Leclerc and Hamilton were separated by 0.056 seconds and both had tales of woe that explained their early exit - but very different ones.

Leclerc said: "Just a very poor qualifying. We are losing one second in the straights which makes it difficult enough already, and then I did a mistake when I had to put the lap in in Q2, following multiple mistakes we have done as a team and this we need to look at because it builds a lot of frustration that doesn't help.

Hamilton added: "It was a nightmare. That wasn't great. So everything wasn't great.

"We knew we would struggle a bit here but maybe more than we anticipated."

You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.

A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.

"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.

There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.

Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream" , external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.

"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."

Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.

Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.

The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.

The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.

Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.

Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.

"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.

"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.

"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.

"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.

"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.

"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."

Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.

"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."

While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.

"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.

In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.

"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.

"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."

A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.

Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.

Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.

The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.

And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.

For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.

Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.

That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.

So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?…

Lewis Hamilton says there is "definitely not" a trust problem between him and his Ferrari team.

The seven-time champion has twice in the past four races ignored a call to pit for fresh tyres, both times to his competitive disadvantage.

The most recent time, in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on 8 November, Hamilton stayed out on worn slick tyres in worsening rain and ended up spinning before pitting on the next lap.

Before this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, Hamilton spoke positively of his relationship with his race engineer Carlo Santi.

"We're constantly working on our communication," said Hamilton, who had a different race engineer last year.

"It's been a lot better this year. Carlos (sic) has done an amazing job. And those particular two times, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed. I got the call right at the last minute.

"We'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united in what's working, in the right direction."

The previous time Hamilton ignored a call to pit was in Singapore, when he decided to stay out during a virtual safety car period. He later apologised .

At the following race in Austin, he explained that he was "always looking at ways to win, always looking at doing potentially something different. And I wanted to be on a different strategy, not just the same strategy as Charles (Leclerc), where we just follow each other".

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem is planning to end age limits for office holders in motorsport's governing body.

The move, which has been proposed for approval at next month's FIA General Assembly, comes six months after Ben Sulayem ended term limits for those holding leadership posts across the organisation .

The FIA statutes currently rule out anyone over the age of 75 from standing as part of a presidential team.

Critics say it is the latest step by Ben Sulayem as he seeks to ensure he can remain FIA president for life.

The proposal to be put forward to the General Assembly, which has been seen by BBC Sport, argues that "age limits could restrict the number of qualified candidates eligible for election by the competent bodies, in particular individuals whose experience and expertise could be of benefit to the FIA".

An age limit of 70 was imposed in 2023, during Ben Sulayem's first presidential term.

It was a tactic to prevent MotorsportUK boss David Richards from being able to oppose Ben Sulayem at the 2025 presidential election.

At the time, Ben Sulayem, who is 64, argued that this would "enhance governance and accountability within the organisation".

The FIA added that the move to introduce an age limit "reflected the FIA's commitment to maintaining high standards in its leadership and governance structures".

Asked why the body had now changed its position, an FIA spokesperson said: "The proposal to remove age limits for FIA officeholders brings the FIA in line with organisations such as the BBC, whose chairman is 74.

"It was approved by the world councils for submission in line with the process set out in the FIA statutes, and will only take effect if the general assembly votes in favour.

"An age limit excludes candidates solely on the basis of their date of birth, regardless of their experience, expertise, or ability to contribute.

"Ultimately, the competent FIA bodies will retain full authority to elect the officeholders they deem appropriate."

Ben Sulayem's move comes in the context of a European Parliament resolution passed in October 2025 on "the role of EU policies in shaping the European Sport Model" , external .

This includes a clause that "recognises that the autonomy of sport is conditional upon good governance, and calls on international, European, and national sports organisations, as well as stakeholder-representative organisations, to implement the highest standards of governance, integrity and transparency, with appropriate checks and balances to ensure accountability".

A consultation on the topic , external , launched in April 2026, is due to report by the end of this year.

The EU's aim is to "tackle the major challenges facing the sport sector. These include financial sustainability and inequalities, governance issues, volunteering decline and inclusion. The goal is to address these challenges through coordinated action at European level."

The FIA age limit was raised to 75 in 2024 on the basis that it was "modernising the governance of the FIA and ensuring that candidates for the presidency are more aligned with current leadership practices".

Age limits for leaders are not universally common in sports governing bodies. Some implement them to promote renewal, others choose not to, allowing the widest breadth of candidates.

Ben Sulayem was first elected FIA president in 2021 and was re-elected unopposed last December as a consequence of a quirk of the FIA statutes preventing any other candidate from standing.

Three people who wanted to oppose him - including former racing driver Laura Villars and ex-FIA steward Tim Mayer - were blocked from doing so .

Villars is currently engaged in a legal action against Ben Sulayem and the FIA in France challenging its electoral process .

Ben Sulayem's presidency has been marked by a series of controversies on the issues of governance and transparency.

In addition to the removal of term limits, he has introduced statutes reducing accountability and concentrating power in his hands.

And he has fired a series of senior officers who questioned aspects to do with his leadership, including:

the former chief executive officer Natalie Robyn who raised questions about the general governance of the FIA

the head of the audit committee Bertrand Badre, a former head of the World Bank, and the compliance officer who investigated and cleared Ben Sulayem on charges of interfering with two separate aspects of F1 operations

Ben Sulayem's first vice-president for sport, Robert Reid, resigned in April 2025 citing "a fundamental breakdown in governance standards within" the FIA.

At the General Assembly, to be held in Shanghai, Ben Sulayem faces a request by the Ukraine Automobile Federation (FAU) to include on the agenda the issue of violations of the FIA statutes and international sporting code by the Russian Automobile Federation (RAF).

The RAF has opened regional branches in four cities recognised as sovereign areas of Ukraine by the United Nations.

The FAU has already asked the FIA to look into the issue through its court of appeal but has received no response.

The FAU is asking the FIA to suspend the RAF's membership of the international body until it closes all its offices in Ukraine and suspends all activity there.

FAU president Oleksander Feldman said: "Our proposal is fully consistent with the position of the International Olympic Committee regarding the conditions for the participation of Russian athletes in competitions.

"Indeed, such participation became possible specifically on the basis of guarantees provided by the Russian Olympic Committee that it would not conduct activities on the sovereign territory of Ukraine."

Formula 1's governing body the FIA is to introduce permanent race stewards from the 2027 season.

The move follows consistent calls from grand prix drivers for the change because of criticisms of inconsistency of decisions regarding penalties for on-track incidents.

The FIA said in a statement that it would begin recruiting permanent stewards, and was planning a "phased introduction" during the 2027 season.

The FIA statement added: "The introduction of dedicated full-time stewards to the FIA's flagship championship will provide continuity and expertise within the stewarding structure, further advancing the FIA's commitment to fairness through the ongoing review and continuous improvement of sporting regulations and stewarding guidelines.

"It will also allow for deeper implementation of best practice and greater consistency in decision-making."

It said that the use of driver stewards, usually an ex-F1 driver, would continue, "recognising the invaluable expertise they bring".

The plan is for "a small number" of full-time stewards to be recruited during 2027 and the group to be expanded from 2028.

"Existing FIA stewards will continue to play a vital role, contributing their experience within a mixed roster of full-time and part-time stewards for the foreseeable future," the statement said.

In reality, the move is not a major step on from the current situation, where a small number of stewards are rotated around races.

Each grand prix has a group of four stewards, one of which is an ex-driver.

Current drivers have often referenced the fact that they had repeatedly complained during briefings with FIA officials that rulings on driver standards and racing errors were not applied on a consistent basis.

Last year, Williams driver Carlos Sainz, a director of drivers' body the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "F1 and the FIA all agree that [permanent stewards] should be the way forward, where at least two of the three stewards are permanent and we have one rotational for teaching purposes."

The decision follows the opening of an FIA race operations centre at F1's Biggin Hill headquarters in south London.

The FIA has in recent years received increased income from F1 - which provides the majority of its funding - on the basis that this would be applied to improving officialdom and rule-making.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said: "This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

Formula 1 bosses are close to a deal that will see V8 turbo hybrid engines replace the current controversial engines in 2030.

McLaren chief executive officer Zak Brown said an "agreement in principle" had been reached by engine manufacturers and F1 bosses on the new rules.

These will be for a 2.1-litre V8 turbo engine with a smaller electrical element than this year, as first revealed by BBC Sport last month.

Some details remain to be resolved but the main core of the rules has been agreed.

The electrical element will be for a maximum power output of 200kW - compared with 350kW this year.

But only half of that will be available at all times, with the remaining half used only for an overtake mode.

A key element of the rules will be to remove the issue of energy starvation that has been criticised by the drivers this year for taking away "pure" racing.

But the overall power output of the engines will be similar to now.

The combustion engine will have about 780bhp, while 200kW is 270bhp.

That means a total power output of 1,050bhp in overtake mode or just over 900bhp in standard running.

Brown said: "Everyone is very, very excited. Now it's about kind of dotting the i's and crossing the t's.

"I'm excited for the new engines, I think everyone will be, the power units. But there's a lot more also going on to continue to evolve the sport. So, between the FIA and Formula 1, they're doing a great job."

Alpine executive director Flavio Briatore said: "We have the agreement, basically. It's not signed, but it looks like everybody's agreed to 2030 V8s, and I'm very happy.

"It's the right way to go. We need an engine with a lot of noise, and a simple engine, and we need to be racing with that."

The ruleset amounts to a compromise reached by manufacturers after FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially pushed for a naturally aspirated engine without turbo or electrical components.

But these were required to reduce overall fuel consumption, and therefore weight at the start of races.

That means Ben Sulayem's desire for a return to the loud volumes of the previous V8 era from 2006 to 2013 will not be achieved. The engines are expected to sound similar to now.

This was important because a significant increase in engine noise would have put at threat some races in city centres that are commercially important to F1, such as Miami and Las Vegas.

The 2.1-litre capacity has been arrived at because it amounts to adding to two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre V6 blocks, with the aim of reducing development costs.

Cars are expected to start races with about 110-120kg of fuel, up from about 100kg now. A total weight limit of 150kg for the power-units will be imposed, down by about 30kg from the current engines.

There will be a fuel energy flow limit to keep the power of the combustion engine under control, and a budget cap figure for engines set at $190m (£145m) per year.

As part of negotiations, General Motors, backers of the Cadillac team, will delay the production of its new engine until 2030. It had been scheduled for 2029.

In return, GM will lose its voting rights on current engine rules and be classified as a new manufacturer from 2030.

The team will continue to use Ferrari customer engines through 2029.

Cadillac F1 chief executive officer Dan Towriss said: "For a period of time, we were working on both. So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8.

"There are a number of designs that are in motion now, and so there's a lot of good foundation for what we're trying to build and the direction we're headed in."

Formula 1 drivers will be limited to a maximum of 27 laps on a set of tyres at next weekend's Qatar Grand Prix.

The decision is caused by concern over the integrity of the Pirelli tyres on the high-speed Lusail track, which has a series of demanding, long-duration corners.

It means teams will have to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap grand prix, as was the case last year.

The limit applies on a single set of tyres whenever it is used across sessions.

So mileage done in practice or qualifying, for example, would limit the number of laps that could be done on a set of tyres in the race.

Pirelli said the limit was longer then last year's 25 laps because of the reduced downforce levels of the 2026 cars compared with 2025.

"The increase has been made possible by the lower load levels recorded so far on the current generation of cars and by a further reinforcement of the tyre construction," a statement said.

Last year, the limit led to a major strategic error by McLaren, who lost a win because they failed to pit under a safety car period when everyone else did.

It is the third time in four years Pirelli has imposed a tyre-duration limit at Qatar, where running wide over flat kerbs in addition to the high-speed nature of the track is especially demanding for the tyres.

Pirelli described the decision as a "precautionary measure" that was "linked to the unique characteristics of the Lusail circuit, which is particularly demanding in terms of energy loads, thermal stress and tread wear".

In terms of the way the limit will be imposed, the statement said: "Laps will be counted cumulatively across all track sessions, including any laps completed under the safety car or virtual safety car.

"As far as the grand prix is concerned, all laps completed from the start signal to the chequered flag will count towards the total.

"Reconnaissance laps, formation laps and any laps completed after the end of the race will not be included.

"In all other track sessions, any lap that has been started but not completed will nevertheless be counted as a full lap.

"Should a team assemble a tyre set using tyres that have covered different mileages, the tyre with the highest lap count will determine the mileage attributed to that set."

The world has been undergoing change in everything from the climate to artificial intelligence — and soon time itself is expected to undergo a major transformation.

As early as 2030, the optical atomic clock is expected to become the primary reference for global timekeeping, redefining the second as an element of time and playing a greater role alongside the conventional atomic clocks now used to maintain Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, standards managed by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (generally known by its French abbreviation B.I.P.M.) in Sèvres, France.

These extraordinarily accurate clocks, scientists say, also eventually would assist and replace some of the atomic clocks now used in telecommunications, satellite navigation and other systems that depend on ultraprecise timing for synchronizing cellphone networks; time stamping financial transactions and tracking the movement of airplanes, cars and ships around the world.

In the countdown to the shift, optical atomic clocks are in production at many universities and research institutions as well as a handful of companies — including Rolex, which already has three that it uses to calibrate testing systems and to contribute to the computation of UTC. (According to Rolex’s website, one of the clocks was the first optical atomic clock to take part in the computation of UTC.)

“There are many different types of optical clock and many research groups and start-ups trying to develop or improve them and bring them to market,” Florian Schreck, the coordinator of the AQuRA optical atomic clock consortium, a collaborative project in Europe, said in an email.

While atomic clocks aren’t exactly sluggish — they break a second into about 9 billion parts, which scientists call ticks — their optical counterparts tick hundreds of trillions of times per second and are astoundingly accurate . Researchers say that if an optical atomic clock had started when the universe began, about 14 billion years ago, it would be off by just about one second today.

When we’re in school, we hear a lot about propaganda. American history textbooks show us political cartoons from the late 19th and early 20th century about the abolition of slavery, the rise of industrial robber-barons, and the progressive movement. European art historians discuss how Louis XIV used paintings and sculptures to present himself as the “Sun King” as he strengthened the power of the French crown over the First and Second Estates. In my own Roman history classes, I spend multiple weeks demonstrating how the emperors employed literature, history, sculpture, and construction projects to assert the supremacy of both Rome and the imperial household. Whether in middle school, high school, or college, students regularly grapple with propaganda in their history classes, learning how people with access to communicative resources have been able to present their own version of reality to sway public opinion in their favor.

Once we’re out of school, though, propaganda falls by the wayside, and ceases to be a concern. It exists, in the public consciousness at least, not as a part of our lives, but as a historical oddity, the behavior of a bygone era — or, when it’s acknowledged in the modern world, as something that happens in the nebulous “over there,” not “here.” And yet, what else can we call the flood of political advertisements in every commercial break that made the World Series borderline unwatchable if not propaganda? After all, are they not trying to sell their version of reality, as opposed to that of their opponents, in an effort to sway voters?

Propaganda is most often understood in terms of politics, but it doesn’t have to be. And right now, we’re living in what I call a sports propaganda moment, as two major entities — the NCAA and Major League Baseball — have gone on the figurative warpath, spending millions of dollars in advertising not to get people to watch their product, but to generate outrage from fans on their own behalf against that of their players.

Whether you’re a fan of a power conference school who competes for the national championship every year or a small liberal arts college who celebrates when their team gets blown out during the March Madness tournament because that meant they made it in the first place, you’ve almost certainly been exposed to commercials sponsored by the Saving College Sports organization in support of the Protect College Sports Act. Since the start of the 2026 college football season (and in truth, since last bowl season, as commercials in support of the bill ran even before it was officially introduced in Congress back in June), they have run a massive ad campaign encouraging fans to contact their congressional representatives and pressure them to vote yes on the bill. Backed by multi-million athletic programs and employing household names such as Deion Sanders and Nick Saban (a current coach and a former one, respectively), these ads center the conversation about the bill on the legitimate concerns fans have about today’s Wild West NIL era — namely, the constant transfers — while ignoring the fact that the bill attempts to, as much as legally possible, reassert the extreme levels of control that the conferences and schools used to have over their athletes.

Starting in the middle of the summer, Major League Baseball has rolled out their own ad campaign in preparation for the upcoming lockout, which is now just a week and a half away. Focused on MLB.tv and social media, the “Level the Playing Field” campaign directly argues for the implementation of a salary cap and floor, claiming that the league cannot have competitive balance due to the payroll disparities that exist between small- and large-market teams. These ads ran all summer, during the All-Star Game festivities, the postseason, the World Series, and the awards season. While, ironically, this meant that t he league plastered everywhere a chart in which the team with the second-highest payroll, the Mets, missed the playoffs as the team with the second-lowest payroll, the Rays, won the pennant, the very fact that the league spent time and energy publicly fighting the players during what should be the biggest annual celebrations of the sport is a testament to their priorities — and the important role that these ads played in their pre-lockout preparations.

Now, obviously, these two situations aren’t 100 percent comparable. Decades of corruption and a refusal to negotiate common sense solutions with its players forced college athletes to turn to the courts for assistance, and once the courts got involved, federal involvement and oversight was all but guaranteed, and all the political machinations that entails. Major League Baseball, meanwhile, is attempting, for the second time this decade, to use the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement as an opportunity to break the power of the players’ union and implement the salary cap that they believe will see franchise values skyrocket . Sure, the almighty dollar may be the driving force for both the NCAA and MLB — both the Protect College Sports Act and the salary cap are, at their core, attempts to rein payrolls in and ensure cost certainty — but each organization is so fundamentally different from the other that their financial systems are incomparable.

Nonetheless, the fact that both collegiate athletics and professional baseball have adopted the same tactic, large-scale propaganda campaigns meant to turn the fans against the players, reflects the unique historical moment we are in. The inaugural manager of the Yankees, Clark Griffith is a titanic figure in the early history of baseball.

Though Clark Griffith is the first man to manage the New York baseball team we now call the Yankees, his time in New York is merely one chapter in a story of one of the giants of baseball’s early history. That’s no shot at Griffith’s time in New York and his importance to the franchise. It’s just he had such an amazing life and career.

He was already an accomplished hurler when he came to New York and became the player-manager of the club, in its first season in The Big Apple. And long after he hung up his cleats, he remained an integral part of baseball in the first half of the 20th century.

Clark Calvin Griffith Born: November 20, 1869 (Clear Creek, MO) Died: October 27, 1955 (Washington, DC) Yankees Tenure: 1903-07 (player/manager), 1908 (manager)

Clark Griffith was already a grizzled veteran when American League President Ban Johnson named him manager of the New York Highlanders (often called the Americans in the press) prior to the 1903 season. It was the inaugural campaign for the club, which relocated from Baltimore after the Orioles folded following two seasons.

The diminutive Griffith (listed at 5-foot-6) was a right-handed pitcher, and a good one, at that. Between 1894 and 1901, he won at least 20 games in a season seven times. His first season in New York was also his last one as a starting pitcher, and he tossed more than 200 innings while managing the club to a disappointing fourth-place finish.

Griffith’s pitching days were not over, however. He transitioned to the bullpen and continued to pitch at a high level while trying to steer the Highlanders to a pennant. In 1904 and 1906, he came close, with the club finishing in second place each season, mere games from wining the American League.

Modern Yankee fans are used to skipper Aaron Boone getting himself tossed from games, though he was shockingly well-behaved in 2026. He’s far from the first Yankee manager to get the hook, of course. Griffith, by virtue of being the first manager, gets that honor. Like his modern successor, Griffith also got himself suspended for his conduct toward umpires.

On Monday, August 27th, 1906, Griffith took umbrage with a safe call at first base while playing St. Louis. As a result, the umpires ordered Griffith off the field. The Highlanders’ skipper took his sweet time about it. Unfortunately for him, AL President Johnson was in the crowd, and the next day he suspended Griffith indefinitely. Yeesh. “Savages in the Box,” this was not. Seems a little harsh. But wait — there’s more. The indefinite suspension might have something to do with Griffith fighting umpire Tim Hurst earlier in the season, which also got him suspended. For that round of fisticuffs, Griffith received a five-day suspension. His ban in August lasted a week.

The Highlanders bottomed out on Griffith’s watch in 1908, and in June he decided it was time for him to move on. Owner Frank J. Farrell tried to dissuade the disheartened Griffith, but to no avail.

“It was fighting against fate,” Griffith told The New York Times , “And I knew when I had enough. I do not know who my successor will be, but I understand [Kid] Elberfeld is mentioned for the place. If that is so, I wish him the best of luck, and I hope my successor will pull the team out of the rut and place them where they belong.”

Griffith’s warm feelings for the club definitely did not last forever. At his death, the Times noted, “Mr. Griffith had two pet dislikes in his lifetime. One was John McGraw and the other was the New York Yankees.”

Griffith’s time in baseball was by no means done when he left New York. Most famously, he eventually found himself in Washington, where he leveraged his assets to obtain a 10 percent stake in the notoriously bad Senators. “First in war; first in peace, and last in the American League,” the old saying went.

Griffith won five pennants in nine years before again relying on his assets to buy a majority share in the franchise. By 1920, he’d transitioned out of the dugout and into the owner’s box, ending a 20-year managerial career where he won 1,491 games (26th most all-time). In 1924, his Senators finally won the World Series, upsetting the New York Giants. They would win further pennants in 1925 and 1933 as well.

Clark Griffith is almost certainly the most important person in the history of Washington baseball, with all due respect to Walter Johnson. He’s also the answer to an obscure yet important bit of trivia. Who was responsible for the tradition of US presidents throwing out the first pitch? It was Griffith, who in 1910 asked President William Howard Taft to toss out the first ball. Taft obliged and the rest is history.

Griffith was also key to baseball’s relationship with the U.S. government and military during both world wars. In World War I, he organized an initiative to get baseball equipment for every American soldier overseas. He even got President Woodrow Wilson to chip in. During World War II, he was one of the people who helped convince President Franklin Roosevelt to keep baseball playing.

He’s the only man in baseball history to have played, managed, and owned a team for at least 20 years each. Clark Griffith was elected to the Major League Baseball Hall of Fame in 1946. His Senators would eventually pass to his son, Calvin, who would move them to Minnesota in 1961 to become the Twins (and become rather infamous in his own right).

Clark Griffith died on October 27, 1955, in Washington, D.C. In its obituary for the legend, The New York Times noted what former president Harry S. Truman had said about Griffith in 1946 when he had thrown out a presidential first pitch, the tradition Griffith started decades earlier.

George Lombard Jr. experienced the highs and lows of a rookie season.

Few positions, or the players manning them, have been debated as intensely as shortstop for the New York Yankees over the last several seasons. Heading into 2026, many fans hoped the club would find a way to move on from the Anthony Volpe experience. However, the club made no external moves and started the season with José Caballero slotted in at the position as the team waited for a rehabbing Volpe to return.

Along the way, injuries and performance, both struggles by the incumbents and red-hot play in the minors, led the Yankees to hand the reins at shortstop over to 21-year-old George Lombard Jr. The rookie would spend August, September, and October at shortstop for the Yankees in what really is the throne of NYC.

In terms of how it went, the staff here at PSA averaged out to a B-minus. In academic speak, that would mean Lombard understood the core material and performed above average, but did not master the assignment.

2026 Stats: 42 G, 166 PA, 23 R, 36 H, 4 2B, 1 3B, 7 HR, 22 RBI, 2 SB, .237/.285/.414, 92 OPS+, 93 wRC+, 0.4 fWAR, 1.1 bWAR.

2027 Contract Status: Pre-arbitration eligible.

Before reaching the show, Lombard was on an absolute tear in the minors. Starting the season in Double-A, he hit .312 with a .971 OPS in 20 games, which earned him a ticket to Scranton. Lombard’s season looked like it might be coming off the rails after an adjustment period, and then he sprained two fingers, which sidelined him for a month and caused him to miss the MLB Futures Game. However, he came back in mid-July and forced the Yankees’ hand right before the Trade Deadline, going on a 14-game heater to the tune of a .377 average, .477 OBP, and 1.081 OPS.

On August 4th, after surviving the Trade Deadline himself, and with the Yankees not acquiring an outside option at shortstop, the club called Lombard up to the show. The kid finished the minor league season slashing .284/.411/.498 with 12 home runs. This performance led Baseball America to name him the Yankees’ Minor League Player of the Year for 2026.

Lombard’s 2026 season at the professional level, and the basis for our grading, really is a story of three parts. The first was a euphoric honeymoon stage. Lombard committed just one error in his first 14 games and racked up eight Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) in his first 100 innings, looking like a potential Platinum Glove winner. This all came as he homered in his first pro at-bat and slashed .320/.393/.560 with a .953 OPS across his first 25 at-bats. It was too good to be true.

After the rise came the fall, as Lombard slumped with the glove and bat. In late August, Lombard made the wrong kind of history, committing an error in six straight games and tying a 105-year-old franchise record. With the stick, big league pitchers started getting him to chase and roll over breaking balls, causing his average to sink to .217 by mid-September. The vibes from some fans really went from “next” to “next Volpe.”

To the kid’s credit, he righted the ship down the stretch and saved himself in the third act. From September 9th through the end of the regular season, Lombard’s defense stabilized to league average, and he hit five home runs in his final 16 games. He carried that confidence into the postseason, going 3-for-4 in the Wild Card opener against Boston and finishing October batting .333 (6-for-18), albeit with an error in the ALDS.

I’ll save the hype train for future preview articles. However, despite only having an 86 mph average exit velocity, Lombard finished the season pacing for 27 home runs over 162 games. There’s also a lot of room for growth, as Lombard had a 17.3 percent walk rate at Triple-A and only a six percent rate in the majors through his first 42 games, or essentially a quarter of a season. The defense, especially when playing beside a big league-quality third baseman, was fine for someone who was just a few months into being able to buy an adult beverage.

Lombard’s minor league season was an A+, while his rookie season comes in at a B-. With some growing pains behind us and a few more likely ahead, here’s to hoping Lombard can continue to improve and develop into a difference-maker. What grade would you circle in red for Lombard’s 2026 season, and what do you predict he’s produce next season?
