The Yankees bring back an old friend to bolster the bullpen.

So far this winter, the bullpen has been a clear priority for the Yankees, who saw no fewer than four important relievers from the 2026 season become free agents. After re-signing Tim Hill and bringing back David Bednar on the qualifying offer, the team has now made its third addition to the bullpen, coming to terms with old friend Jonathan Loáisiga on a two-year deal with a team option for 2029.

Canal 4 News in Loáisiga’s native Nicaragua had the news late last night, the man himself hinted at it with a picture of the NYC skyline on his Instagram story , and Jorge Castillo of ESPN confirmed it this morning. MLB.com’s Mark Feinsand reported the total outlay of the contract as $18 million across the two years and buyout.

Yankees fans are, of course, very familiar with the man nicknamed Johnny Lasagna. Signed as a minor-league free agent in 2016 after a couple years in the Giants’ organization, Loáisiga spent parts of eight seasons with the big league club, and served as the bullpen’s ace fireman/setup man in 2021 and the second half of 2022. Injuries and ineffectiveness plagued the right-hander for the next three seasons, however, and after a lackluster 2025, the Bombers declined his team option for 2026.

It turned out to be the best thing for him. After sitting on the market for most of the winter, Loáisiga signed a minor-league free agent deal with the Diamondbacks last January. He made the team out of spring training, stayed healthy for a full season for the first time in five years, and put together one of the best seasons of his career, posting a 2.42 ERA in 67 innings. Perhaps more importantly, his advanced metrics were some of the best of his career, and helps explain why there were so many suitors for the recently-turned 32-year-old (the Mets, Phillies, Dodgers, and Blue Jays were all reportedly in on him).

Despite the small time apart, though, Loáisiga is not exactly the same pitcher who Yankee fans remember. Gone are the days where he threw the sinker like Mariano Rivera threw the cutter, i.e., pretty much every pitch. Although it’s still his main offering (he threw it 35 percent of the time last year), that is a far cry from the 54-to-69-percent usage rates from his first Yankees stint; in its stead, he’s upped his changeup, fastball, and cutter.

While nobody would ever consider Loáisiga a strikeout pitcher, these changes oversaw a slight bump in strikeout percentage to 18.4 percent from his 16.6-percent rate between 2022-24 and a slight drop in walk rate to a career-best 5.0 percent, all without sacrificing ground-ball rate. The question will just be how his body holds up after an actual full, healthy season.

Even with Loáisiga, Hill, and Bednar back in the fold, the Yankees are probably not yet done looking at bullpen arms — assuming they ever truly feel like they have enough bullpen arms. At this point, though, the Yankees have successfully turned it from a “need” to a “want,” as they’re no longer so thin out there that Yerry De los Santos and Angel Chivilli were listed as two of the team’s higher-leverage relief arms on the FanGraphs Depth Chart .

One could, of course, absolutely still argue that they still need a big swing-and-miss arm in the ’pen, as they’re still lacking in that regard and not everyone should be a pitch-to-contact guy. As we wait for the league to come to a screeching halt in 10 days due to the owners’ insistence on a lockout, getting some things crossed off the winter to-do list is certainly not a bad thing, and Loáisiga checks another box.

Cruz and Gil become free agents while the Yankees’ other seven arbitration-eligible players were tendered contracts.

The deadline to tender contracts to arbitration-eligible players arrived at 5pm ET on November 20th, and the Yankees have decided to non-tender Fernando Cruz and Luis Gil. The pair of right-handed pitchers become free agents, while Luis García Jr., Anthony Volpe, Ryan Weathers, Clarke Schmidt, Austin Wells, José Caballero, and Heliot Ramos have the next few months to decide whether to accept the Yankees’ offer or submit their own offers as the initial step in negotiating a salary for 2027.

Should both parties fail to agree on a number, the case would be submitted to an arbitration hearing. These hearings typically occur in February — subject to change due to the looming expiry of the CBA and expected owner lockout of the players — with the arbitration panel resolving the case by awarding the figure tendered by either the club or the player as opposed to a midpoint of those two figures.

The decision to non-tender Cruz and Gil does not come as much of a surprise. Both players were tabbed to earn $2.3 million in 2027 according to MLB Trade Rumors’ arbitration projections — an affordable amount that the Yankees nonetheless decided was better spent elsewhere given the question marks surrounding both players’ health and effectiveness going forward. It is the second year in the row that the Yankees have used the non-tender as a way to clear roster space on the pitching side. In 2025, they non-tendered five pitchers — Mark Leiter Jr., Ian Hamilton, Scott Effross, Jake Cousins, and Michael Arias — out of their 14 arbitration-eligible players.

Our own Andrés Chávez identified Gil as a non-tender candidate at the beginning of the month. It has been a precipitous fall from the stratospheric seven-start stretch that ultimately won Gil the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year Award. He has battled lat and shoulder injuries over the past two seasons, limiting him to 20 appearances (15 starts) with a 3.74 ERA, 5.44 FIP, and 58 strikeouts in 84.1 innings. An alarming loss of velocity on his fastball and worsening command has seen his strikeout rate crater from 27.3-percent between 2021-2024 to just 15.8-percent in the last two years, creating an untenable 1.9-percent strikeout-minus-walk ratio. There were question whether Gil might rediscover some effectiveness in a max-effort bullpen role, but ultimately the Yankees decided that the experiment wasn’t worth the effort. In five big league seasons with the Yankees, Gil went 21-11 in 56 appearances (51 starts), posting a 3.61 ERA, 4.54 FIP, 272 strikeouts, and 2.8 fWAR in 269.1 innings.

As for Cruz, the righty reliever became something of a cult hero thanks to his devastating splitter and enthusiastic celebrations. Arriving via trade from the Reds in the 2024-25 offseason, Cruz carved out a late-inning high leverage role by posting a 32-percent strikeout rate thanks to the splitter that allowed him to sit at the very top of the league whiff rate leaderboard. However, his appearances waned across his final two months of action in 2026, and it was subsequently revealed that he had suffered a partial tear of his UCL. The injury ended his campaign despite Cruz opting not to undergo surgery in the hope of making a late-season comeback. He was recently able to begin a throwing program, and GM Brian Cashman expressed optimism about his availability in 2027, but it appears the medicals on his elbow were scary enough to not be worth the risk at that price. In two seasons with the Yankees, Cruz made 110 relief appearances, pitching to a 3.33 ERA and 3.71 FIP with 139 strikeouts and 1.2 fWAR in 102.2 innings.

It is no surprise that the Yankees tendered contracts to the remaining seven arbitration-eligible players. The only other plausible candidate for non-tender was Schmidt, who is projected to earn $4.5 million in his third and final year of arbitration eligibility. The 30-year-old righty has missed significant parts of the last three seasons to injury — a lat strain in 2024, Tommy John surgery in 2025, and a biceps injury shortly after his return from Tommy John rehab in 2026. In total, he has made just 30 starts since the start of 2024, pitching just 164.2 innings after tossing a career-high 159 in 2023. However, Cashman confirmed that Schmidt is fully healthy entering this offseason, and the righty offers a much high floor and ceiling than Gil as starting rotation depth while also representing an intriguing multi-inning relief option.

With Cruz and Gil’s non-tenders, the Yankees have now subtracted two more arms from their already depleted relief corps. David Bednar did choose to return on the qualifying offer while the team has also reunited with Tim Hill and Jonathan Loáisiga in recent days, but there remains a good deal of work to be done to fill out the big-leaguer bullpen. There also remains the possibility that the Yankees could reintegrate Cruz and Gil on minor-league deals in the coming days.

Two Atlantic Division foes haven’t been the Knicks in four years. Think about that.

As mentioned on last night’s broadcast, it’s hard to believe such a dominant stretch existed against a longtime rival that has been the Eastern Conference’s banner of success for generations.

Simply, the sport is cyclical, and the few times the Celtics were in the doldrums, the Knicks were contending for titles. Through the many dark ages of Knicks history, the Celtics dominated. It’s why they’ve only faced off in the postseason three times in the last 35 years.

From 1965-67, the Celtics won 21 in a row against the Knicks in the heart of the Bill Russell era. It took 25 years to return the favor.

On January 10, 1993, the Celtics outlasted the Knicks at TD Garden in a 100-97 win. They wouldn’t win another game in this rivalry for over five years.

The Celtics won 48 games in 1992-93, but quickly fell into the East’s cellar. They wouldn’t win 40 games again in a season until 2001-02, while at the same time, Patrick Ewing and the Knicks had only the Bulls and Pacers competing with them for spots in the NBA Finals yearly.

Ewing would score 65 combined over the next two meetings in April 1993 before scoring 30 again on Opening Night that October in a three-point win in Boston. He routinely owned the Celtics during this time, reaching a crescendo with a 36-14 effort in March 1994.

As the Celtics got worse, the Knicks took advantage of them more and more. A 35-point blowout in February 1994 still stands as one of the biggest blowouts in the rivalry’s history. Hubert Davis nailed five threes and scored 25 points in a 90-83 win the following month.

It was always a different enemy that flummoxed the Celtics. Charles Smith scoring 25, Anthony Mason scoring 21, and John Starks and Ewing’s consistency. Even as Pat Riley turned into Jeff Van Gundy, the Knicks never lost a step.

The streak had reached 17 by January 28, 1997, when the pitiful 9-30 Celtics put the greatest scare into the contending Knicks yet. An eight-point lead in the final minutes dwindled to a tie on a Todd Day three in the final minute before free throws by Antoine Walker gave Boston the lead in the final minute.

Just when the streak appeared over, Chris Childs called game with eight seconds left.

Eventually, the streak would finally end on January 26, 1998, when the Knicks were held to just 85 points behind a 25-point gem by Chauncey Billups. Even this triumphant victory came with an asterisk, as Ewing missed the game due to wrist surgery. Huh.

The Knicks own the Cavs in the playoffs, but did you know there was a stretch they owned them like this?

In five all-time playoff meetings, the Knicks are 16-2 against the Cavs, but once took things to another level in the early 1980s.

Unlike the Celtics, this is pretty peculiar. The Knicks were an average team during this streak, but took advantage of one of the worst eras of Cavs basketball under Ted Stepien.

Quite precisely, this streak can be known as the “Stepien Streak”, as while he was owner from April 1980 to his sale in April 1983, the Cavs went 1-16 against the Knicks, with the lone win coming just two weeks before he sold the team in late March of 1983.

Highlights of the streak include Mike Glenn’s 29-point game in November 1980 (second-highest scoring game of his career), Ray Williams’ 37-point gem in an overtime win two weeks later, and perennially playing in front of 4,000 fans at an empty Richfield Coliseum. The NBA was totally different in the 80s.

Back in the day, there weren’t many teams. As such, you get stuff like this.

Over a span of 400 days from February 6, 1952, to March 11, 1953, the Knicks played the Baltimore Bullets 17 times and won every single one of them.

The 1950s Knicks can sometimes be referred to as the Silver Era of Knicks basketball due to the team making multiple Finals appearances before Russell came and made the East his own, so it’s no surprise they were dominant. But like this?

The lore of 1950s NBA is quite fascinating. These teams played each other three times in six days in February 1952 when the streak began, but played the games in three different places. The Bullets won 82-81 in the Baltimore Coliseum on February 4, the Knicks won 73-70 at the 69th Regiment Armory on February 6, and the two teams met in Philadelphia on February 8 in a 20-point blowout win for Ray Lumpp and the Knicks.

On March 5, the teams participated in a doubleheader at the Boston Garden, preceding a game between the Bucks and Celtics later that night.

In 1952-53, when the Knicks went 10-0 against the Bullets en route to a Finals appearance, they played one game in Philly, two games in Boston (one of which went to triple overtime), and even played in Trenton, New Jersey, on March 5, 1953.

Finally, the Bullets snapped the skid on November 14, 1953, behind 19 points by Max Zaslofsky in Baltimore.

Can the Knicks score enough against the league’s best defense?

It wasn’t long ago that a Knicks vs. Timberwolves matchup almost felt like a mini-rivalry—one of the few the Knicks had against a team from the Western Conference.

Given the East Coast vs. West Coast of it all, and the LeBron vs. New York effect, the Lakers made for a fun matchup. The Spurs and Knicks have had some tough battles, including the 1999 Finals and the 2024 Christmas Day game, and that pseudo-rivalry was elevated to a new level with the 2026 Finals. But whenever the Knicks and Timberwolves played each other over the last two seasons, it felt like there was more on the line than just the game. It was a battle for narrative, not just bragging rights. Which team won the Karl-Anthony Towns trade? How would former Knicks Julius Randle and Donte DiVincenzo play against their former team? Now, with the Knicks having won a championship and Randle moving from Minnesota to Brooklyn, this matchup no longer feels as personal.

That doesn’t mean that it’ll be a bad game. Nor does it mean that the Timberwolves won’t be a tough opponent. At 11-4, they enter Thursday night with a better record than the Knicks despite being without star guard Anthony Edwards since he underwent knee surgery on October 29. And contrary to expectations, their success hasn’t been a result of LaMelo Ball putting up insane offensive numbers. Their scoring has been incredibly balanced, with Ayo Dosunmu averaging 18.6 PPG, Ball averaging 17.7 PPG, and Jaden McDaniels averaging 17.1 PPG. Even without a single player averaging more than 20 PPG, they’ve managed to have the 12th-highest offensive rating.

Where they’ve remained elite sans Edwards, though, is on the defensive end. The Timberwolves, thanks in large part to four-time Defensive Player of the Year winner Rudy Gobert, have been incredibly dominant defensively. As of today, they have the best defensive rating in the league at 104, two full points better than the second-place Celtics. They rank third in the league in opponents’ field goal percentage, first in opponents’ three-point percentage, and force the sixth-most turnovers per game.

The Knicks, who haven’t completely gotten past their early-season shooting struggles, may have a tough time scoring against the Timberwolves. Even with the recent play of Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Landry Shamet, and Miles McBride supplementing Karl-Anthony Towns’ dominant season, the Knicks still find themselves outside the top 10 in three-point percentage and near the bottom of the league in field goal percentage. That doesn’t mean the Knicks won’t be able to score, though. They have two very clear advantages heading into tonight.

One advantage is that they’ll have the two best players on the court. The Knicks can say this in a lot of games, and that hasn’t stopped them from getting off to a disappointing 8-6 start. And this matters less in the regular season than it does in the postseason. But this should still bode well for the Knicks. Brunson won Eastern Conference Player of the Week to kick off November and hasn’t really looked back. Even against a tough Raptors defense, he came through and put together back-to-back quality games. And you can make the argument that Towns hasn’t had a single game this season where he hasn’t been great in one way or another. The big man has also had some monstrous games against his former team, averaging 29.0 PPG, 14.3 RPG, and 3.7 APG while shooting 61.7% from the field and 56.3% from three. And in two of those three games, Towns scored 32 or more points and grabbed 13 or more rebounds.

The Knicks’ second advantage comes on the offensive boards. The Timberwolves give up the 12th-most offensive rebounds per game. Some of that is a direct result of their defense forcing so many misses. But with the Knicks being a top-five offensive rebounding team, Towns, as well as Andre Drummond and even Jordan Clarkson, could have big nights on the boards, making up for what could be an inefficient shooting night.

This will be a good test for a Knicks team that has earned seven of its eight wins against teams that are .500 or worse. The Timberwolves are 7-2 at home, deploy a dominant defense predicated on forcing players into the rim-protecting monster that is Gobert, and have a balanced offense that often scores just enough points. But expect the Knicks to lean on their two big horses. Brunson has also had some nice games against the Timberwolves and LaMelo Ball-led teams. And Towns has dominated just about everybody this season. We also can’t forget that the Knicks themselves have a good defense, which could test a limited Timberwolves offense. Knicks welcome a surprising Portland team at the Garden on Saturday night.

As we all know, Madison Square Garden isn’t just the most glorious gymnasium on the planet and revered in the world of sports; it’s also famous for the long list of famous musicians who have performed under its unique bicycle-wheel ceiling. Now the Portland Trail Blazers are dropping by for a quick game of hoops on Saturday night, but they might actually be the one franchise that would be adept at bringing out the microphones as well. I mean, who wouldn’t want to hear the newest rendition of all-timers like “Bust A Bucket” or “Rip City Rhapsody” ?!

Not to disappoint anybody, but the days of Terry Porter and those shiny lycra dance outfits of the Blazers cheerleaders that would have made Cory Everson proud are long gone. Today’s Rip City Rascals (coming in at 10-5) have their own way of entertaining a crowd, though, which is more than many would have expected before the season. With the return of Damian Lillard and a highly questionable move for “Pistol Petey” Ja Morant, the Blazers looked to be about five years late to the modern NBA party but atleast early it turns out they are anything but.

New head coach Micah Nori is making one of the more funky-looking rosters in the Association work so far, and he does it with a very modern, analytical approach. The Blazers shoot and make way more threes than their opponents (outscoring them by about 12+ points from beyond the arc), defend downtown better than 25 other teams in the NBA, and make sure Tony Brothers and his brothers-in-arms in the striped shirts have a living by drawing the second most fouls in the league.

Most of those foul numbers might be attributed to Deni Avdija. Only Luka from the Lakers and that feaky Greek in Miami stand at the charity stripe more frequently than the Israeli All-Star from Portland, leading to some fans questioning the ethics in his basketball bravado. But make no mistake about it, he is a serious talent, big-bodied and confident with a well-rounded game that can give every opponent problems. If he will be of any concern to the Knicks is not clear yet though; Avdija missed Portland’s last two with a foot injury and figures to be a game-time decision.

But even without Avdija, Portland (road record 7-3) will present a very interesting matchup for your Knickerbockers. Damian Lillard seems to be rejuvenated after his Achilles injury, and a lot about his game feels a bit more wholesome in the jersey in which he always belonged. Behind him you have a Jrue Holiday coming off the bench, probably one of the more professional, classy guys you can find in the NBA these days. Cheekily, he also still packs quite a punch in his game, giving Nori first-class playmaking, tough D, and leadership in spades. If you think rattling these two old wily pros might get you anywhere, think again.

You could have more luck with some of the younger Blazers, but many of them bring certain elite skills to the table, too. Belgian baller Toumani Camara is one of the best defenders in the entire league, long, lanky, and extremely athletic. Seemingly plodding big man Donovan Clingan is getting more mobile by the minute and still hasn’t lost his knack for gobbling up boards like a motivated Moses Malone did back in the day. Sidy Cissoko is another promising young wing, and former number two overall pick Scoot Henderson, while having a nightmarish season overall, can still break out for a big one as he did against Milwaukee the other night with 27 points.

What all those Blazers have in common is that they buy into Nori’s system so far and operate with a clear-cut plan on the shiny hardwood. They extend their defense, making it hard to find anything downtown but also possible to do some damage in the midrange. On offense, they move the ball well, play five-out as much as they can (using Clingan as a high screen setter), and rely on balanced scoring night in and night out. It’s a good formula, especially without Ja Morant, who has missed all but four games with a hamstring injury so far this year. The Knicks will have to touch the paint plenty to get that Portland defense moving, and they have to attack Lillard whenever possible on that end. Their superior depth could be a factor as well.

If the Blazers then throw a curveball and try to actually upend the Knicks’ three-game winning streak by dragging them into a singing competition after all? No need to worry - we still got Tyler Kolek !

Led by their stars the Knicks make it 15 in a row against Toronto.

One of the more prominent flies caught in the interwebs these days was the nomination of Robert Pattinson as the new lead for the James Bond franchise. Yes, the guy who made daughters melt by the millions about two decades ago and who always looks like the vampire that made him prominent drank all the blood from his veins. Apparently he’s a really good actor, but pardon me if I’m not acting like I’m some kind of wannabe film critic just because I like movies every once in a while.

For my liking, the 007 I loved ended with the retirement of Roger Moore, a second gut punch not needed after the grim realization that Sean Connery’s time in Her Majesty’s Service was over (we ignore Roger Lazenby for obvious reasons). Before watching any of the newer films, I always much rather flopped in one of the classics, because with the world spinning faster every day, there are just some things in life I’d like to stay the way they are. Like that bank account from December before all the insurance companies wish you a happy new year or that favorite dish your Grandma used to make before she discovered light whipping cream. And while we’re at it, the fact that the New York Knicks do not lose to the Toronto Raptors.

After watching the Knicks almost win a carbon copy of their game on Sunday in Toronto for their 15th in a row against the Dinos, it truly feels like some divine decree puts some prehistoric panic on the Raptors in the final minutes and sprinkles just enough calmness on the orange and blue to pull it out in the end. Just like Unmitigated Gall wrote in the celebratory Postgame Thread: “Sayeth the Lord: Let it be 15 straight”. But maybe it’s also just pure and legit NBA talent taking over, and prevailing over the guys who are airballing free throws or thought it was a good idea to give Jakob Poeltl north of 100 million dollars to play basketball.

Even if Jalen Brunson shot it as purely as “The Man with the Golden Gun,” late everything for New York started and ended last night with Karl-Anthony Towns. Early in the season, he looks sharper than Oddjob’s razor-edged hat (shoutout to “Tosh Togo” Harold Sakata) and, on top of it, more powerful than Richard Kiel’s “Jaws”. KAT’s dominance was on full display against a team that could only put defenders on him who were either too small or too slow. Dismantling those adversaries wasn’t even the most impressive thing the 31-year-old did, as his passing at times was as beautiful as Honey Ryder, Tatiana Romanova and Miss Galore combined.

To be serious for a second: It is astonishing how Karl-Anthony Towns has turned around his career after more than a decade in the league. He is by far the most consistent Knick right now, has cut down on his foul issues for the time being, and looks extremely decisive on both ends of the court. In Minnesota, he always gave the impression of lacking professionalism, and now he looks like the most serious player on a team full of guys who seemingly laughed the last time the Raptors or Nets beat the Knicks. Maybe “You only live twice” as a basketball player, but in KAT’s case that looks to be plenty enough.

The “License to Kill” in the end, of course, rests with his buddy about a foot shorter than him. You wouldn’t believe it watching the first half last night as the Raptors’ eyes got as wide seeing Jalen Brunson defend them as Auric Goldfinger’s were when he saw that shiny gold bar on the 18th green at Stoke Park. If there was a possession where Toronto didn’t attack Brunson in the first half, I seriously cannot remember it. The same goes for any offensive possession that didn’t end up with a late shot clock. It was really a desperate look at times, so desperate that Mike Brown even turned to a zone in the second half, called blitzes when Toronto barely crossed midcourt, and gave sparkplug Jose Alvarado the nod late in the third quarter. And as so often in the past, some of that stuff worked (we still do not like those traps, Mikey).

With the game on the line, the Knicks turned into a rolling “Thunderball” that just couldn’t be stopped. Mikal Bridges locked down on defense for the second straight game, the backup point guard duelists provided numerous little plays, OG Anunoby smiled, and Landry Shamet once again looked like some cool device Q designed in an underground bunker - the red button unleashes movement threes and hellish defense on the opponent. And you have to deal with KAT and Brunson on top of all that? Good luck. When the orange and blue have it going like that, it seems as if they could even make some of those megalomaniac Bond villain plots for world supremacy work. Everything seems possible - even the Captain swatting shots and turning into Jalen Dikembe Mutombo Mpolondo Mukamba Jean-Jacques Wamutombo Brunson. RIP to the legend.

Since “Diamonds Are Forever,” we really do not need a constant reminder of everything these Knicks are capable of; we still remember last year pretty well. That doesn’t mean it does not feel extremely awesome and puts a comfortable calm into a fan’s heart to see them clicking on all cylinders. It would be nice if these cylinders wouldn’t take three quarters to get going, but as long as the Knicks go home with goddess Victory, there’s nothing wrong with things the way they are. Just like there probably is nothing wrong with Robert Pattinson playing James Bond, so let us all wish him well.

And let’s hope for him he’s not a Raptors fan.

NY built a 16-point lead, survived a furious Minny rally, and escaped with a 102-99 win despite a scoreless final 3:26.

The Timberwolves (11-5) have been the talk of the West, especially with their level of success given the absence of star guard Anthony Edwards (knee). Coach Chris Finch has his crew chucking up 116.7 points per game while also leading the league in rebounding and fielding the top defense. So far this season, the Wolves have held every opponent to under 50% from the floor—and they would again tonight. New York (9-6) knew the trouble that awaited them as they squared off with their first Western Conference team of the season. The game started with runs in either direction, but the Knicks gained steam and took a 15-point lead into halftime. In the third quarter, Minnesota chipped away at the lead, and Jaden McDaniels led the doggies on a rally in the fourth quarter to cut the lead to three with a scant few minutes left. But neither team could buy a bucket down the stretch. The Knicks went scoreless for the final three and a half minutes, the T’Wolves missed on everything, and the visitors escaped with a 102-99 victory.

That’s the lowest score for the Wolves this season. Take a bow, fellas.

On a first-quarter drive, LaMelo Ball (your favorite Ball brother?) swiped an arm across Jalen Brunson’s face. Cap was rattled by it and subbed out around the nine-minute mark, giving Tyler Kolek an unusually early appearance. With Jalen out, the visitors went on a 12-0 run. The backup guard was terrific in his first-half play, dishing five dimes in seven minutes, a third of the team’s total, and leading a second unit that tallied 17 first-half points.

A game of runs! Minny responded with a 13-2 run that included Ball attacking the paint for points and Jaden McDaniels swishing from long range. McDaniels was Minnesota’s most efficient scorer in the half, putting up 11 points on perfect 4-of-4 shooting, including three triples (but also three costly turnovers). Returning the favor, Josh Hart dropped a triple that started an 11-3 run and gave New York a 33-26 lead at the break.

In the second quarter, KAT and OG Anunoby stepped further into the spotlight. They combined for 30 first-half points on 12-of-18 shooting. Karl sang beautifully on his former home court, scoring 17 points and hauling in eight boards in just 16 minutes; OG chimed in with 13 points and a pair of blocks. Jose Alvarado got a little run but was quiet in the quarter. In a nice return to form, Josh Hart added nine points on 3-of-4 shooting from deep, while steady-eddie Landry Shamet provided a major lift off the bench with 10 points and a team-best plus-17 in 17 minutes.

The T’Wolves have length that can really clog the lane, and that explains why Jalen Brunson managed just seven points on 2-of-8 shooting, with his two makes coming from the outfield. Against most teams, Cap performs his string music in the paint, but these Minnesota trees make for a dense forest. Also underwhelming: Mikal Bridges, who threw the ball at the basket just once in his 11 minutes before intermission. It’s sort of wild that the Knicks posted 65 first-half points despite getting only nine points from their starting backcourt.

Also weird: Rudy Gobert had just five points and one rebound in his first 15 minutes. In fact, the Wolves’ starting frontcourt of McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga, and Gobert combined for two rebounds. Believe it, Ripley! They weren’t the only stinkers on the home team. Ball, Kuminga, and Ayo Dosunmu combined to shoot 4-of-17 through the half. Minnesota shot a respectable 44% overall and 39% from three, but outside of McDaniels, nobody found much rhythm. With the Knicks shooting a blistering 57% from the field and an eye-popping 63% from deep (10-of-16), the good guys were ahead 65-50 at intermission.

In the third quarter, Brunson shouldered the load, scoring 14 points in the period, and Bridges showed up to sink a three and commit two thefts. Towns continued to crash the glass but cooled off somewhat offensively, as did OG. For the home team, Kuminga poured in 14 points, making two three-pointers while blocking three shots. The Wolves couldn’t put together a sustained run, though. Trailing 83-66 with around 3:30 left, they outscored our heroes 12-7, cutting the score to 90-78 at the break.

To start the final frame, Kolek converted a four-point play to give the guests a 16-point lead. But we never thought the Furballs would roll over and die—and no, they didn’t. As New York’s offense stalled (e.g., Towns missed four of five, which he redeemed with three stuffs), McDaniels, Trey Lyles, and the Wolves chipped away at the lead. After New York went ahead 97-85 with 7:56 remaining, Minnesota scored eight unanswered points, including a McDaniels three and a Ball pull-up triple, to cut the lead to four. The Knicks went nearly four minutes without scoring, prompting a timeout and the return of Bridges and Anunoby.

What makes tonight’s win most stunning is that New York managed to achieve it despite going scoreless over the final 3:26. During that grisly stretch, KAT copped a flopping tech, Gobert slammed an alley-oop, and Ayo buried a three, bringing the Timberwolves within three with 2:34 left. Brunson missed a pull-up jumper, New York committed a shot-clock violation, Towns was called for an offensive foul with 1:04 left, and Bridges missed a turnaround jumper with 23 seconds remaining.

The hosts had plenty of chances to tie or steal the lead but couldn’t capitalize. Ball bricked two shots in the final 1:39; Dosunmu whiffed a bunny; and Bridges blocked Gobert’s putback attempt with 44 seconds left—arguably the biggest defensive play of the game. Ball blanked on a potential tying longball with 10 seconds remaining, and Kuminga collected the rebound but threw the ball away, with Landry Shamet securing the steal to end Minnesota’s night.…

As their beautiful offense waned the Knicks’ D took over against Minnesota.

LaMelo Ball hit one of his patented three-pointers from the left elbow early in the third quarter against the New York Knicks last night and as the crowd cheered, he proceeded to jog back on defense. Of course, the only not totally broken Ball brother couldn’t let the moment pass without completely indulging himself into a thoroughly scripted “ice in the veins”-gesture that feels as original these days as a two-handed set shot. Just a moment later Josh Hart rained on the parade, running directly by Vanilla Ball’s D and finishing an easy backdoor cut with a simple layup. And just like that the Knicks were up 14 again, ignoring the protocol of how cutting a deficit to 12 in a game where your team got handsomely dominated up to that point needs to be celebrated.

It feels good to root for a professional team, doesn’t it? It will allow you to say things like Real Clydes Wear Plaid shared in the Postgame Thread and which I unapologetically stole for the headline of this recap. The Knicks won their third game in a row at Minnesota last night and they probably made it a lot harder than it needed to be. Their opponents certainly had something to do with it, no matter how ill-advised some individual emotions might have been. The Timberwolves can play tremendous defense, are as long as those trees in their logo and have an aggression you could certainly link to that name-giving animal of them. They got a good albeit cranky coach, a proven system, years of winning experience. Yet in the end they also got LaMelo Ball now.

We get that he is a talented, at times iconic passer; we also get that he has found his footing fairly well on the frozen tundra near the Great Lakes so far. But we really can’t get convinced that you can ever really win big with a “talent” like that. His play can remind one of the game young kids play before they really get a hang of Dr. Naismith’s rules. They also take two steps before every dribble, then four after they pick the ball up. They also couldn’t care less about a repetitive shooting motion or dribbling the ball without palming it every time. With the kids it’s okay and fun, we let them discover themselves as players and excuse it. But Lamborghini LaMelo should be held to a different standard, he is supposed to be a professional NBA player after all.

Luckily for the Knicks, they got plenty of real pros on their roster, guys who truly care about winning and treat their profession like it means something - not only to them but to others. It certainly seemed that way when they played most of the game last night with a level of calmness and concentration that has been a hallmark of theirs ever since they went on that beautiful championship run last year. But despite all their dominance over that two-month stretch in the playoffs, you can’t ignore that they are a team with plenty of cracks in their armor, many of which showed themselves last night as well. It’s the kind of weakness that are often the reason for the Bockers falling behind big only to have the opportunity to stage their beloved monumental comebacks later on.

Yesterday the Knicks offense completely bogged down late when Minnesota went to more switching on D (raise your hand if you’ve seen that before), neutralizing all the beautiful team basketball that helped the Gotham Gang run up an almost 20-point lead earlier. Not even Karl-Anthony Towns, once again mesmerizing for most of the night against a traditional five at his old stomping grounds, couldn’t regain his first-half form. Maybe he rode the pine a little long, Mr. Brown? Well, you can’t play him all 48, we get it. A lineup that included Jose Alvarado, Andre Drummond and Josh Hart was still an interesting choice, to say the least. For all the individual chops it’s quite a load for Jalen Brunson to carry that group offensively, it almost feels like him heaving big AD up K2 or some other majestic mountain. It might get you to the summit against certain defenses but considering some defenses are as long and physical as the Wolf Pack, it can also get cold rather quickly. Especially when Brunson still hasn’t found his touch inside the paint yet.

That New York could still pull it out in the end is a testament to timely plays and a gritty, opportunistic defense that at no point in the game relented to the physically imposing Wolves coming at them. When LaMelo Ball couldn’t find someone open downtown, the canines’ only plan was to ram their oversized combo forwards ahead. It worked here or there but never consistently. Watch out, there’s an extended arm coming at you - boom, another offensive foul! It’s an interesting yet understandable choice by the league to make the off arm a point of emphasis this year (sorry, SGA). Why didn’t they do the same for palming the basketball or taking more steps than a dressage horse? Your guess is as good as mine.

For the moment, though, let us not worry about it - there is a win to be celebrated. For all we know though, our guys are probably watching some film right now and preparing for their next opponent (Portland on Saturday). Maybe they are also speeding race cars through some busy pedestrian zone or practice their one-legged step-back fadeaway jumper that has netted them less than 42 percent shooting for their career?

Nah, we leave that to the guy with ice in his veins.

Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.

The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.

The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.

The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.

On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.

The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.

Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.

These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.

He said etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.

These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.

“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”

He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.

“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”

NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.

Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment , which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.

Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.

Job cuts to exclude shop floor, aircraft maintenance and trainees but move prompts calls for more orders to support British defence giant

BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, triggering calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor.

The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”.

The cuts represent about 2% of its 50,000 strong workforce in the UK, which includes about 18,500 in its air business and about 1,000 in its head office in London. They will be made through voluntary redundancies and will exclude people working on the shop floor, aircraft maintenance at RAF bases and early career trainees.

A spokesperson for BAE said the cuts represented the “next stage of our ongoing focus on enhancing our agility and competitiveness, so we can help to maximise the value of every pound our customers spend on defence.

“We recognise that this news may be unsettling for our people and we’re focused on achieving potential workforce reductions through a voluntary process,” they said.

BAE last year received an order for 20 Typhoon fighter jets from Turkey, in a deal announced at the factory by Keir Starmer. However, that order is thought to provide only two years of work at the Lancashire factories – not enough to sustain jobs until production starts on the next generation of fighters. BAE will lead production of the sixth-generation Tempest fighter in an alliance with Italy and Japan.

A source with knowledge of the matter said that the job cuts were linked to uncertainty over the Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet programme , more than cost-cutting.

The move comes even as BAE has benefited from a boom in defence spending since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, the company told its investors it had secured £33bn in orders so far this year and that it expected further contracts before the end of 2026. It also raised its free cashflow guidance for its financial year by 10%, from about £2bn to £3bn.

Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the union Unite, warned that there would not be a manufacturing industry left in the UK “if the government doesn’t start making critical decisions”.

“To stop the erosion of defence jobs and get the growth we need, the government needs to announce contracts for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) immediately,” she said.

BAE unveiled the uncrewed CCA – which is named Brontanax – at the Farnborough International airshow in July.

Andrew Snowden, a Conservative MP in Lancashire where BAE has two air manufacturing hubs, echoed Graham’s call for more government support.

He told the Lancashire Post: “The government should act now to support BAE by placing orders for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft, giving skilled workers and the supply chain here in Lancashire a clear pipeline of work.”

UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash

A ndrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera .

Bailey and his senior managers believe they can modernise the Bank’s Grade I-listed structure and interiors while 3,500 staff are still busy at work on site.

By the summer of 2028, 1,400 Bank staff who work in a nearby office at 20 Moorgate will be relocated to Threadneedle Street, have taken voluntary redundancy or have been offered an alternative job in a new outpost in Leeds, also being refurbished.

It appears a unique project for Britain’s struggling building trade: overhaul a site with a globally recognised exterior; preserve its Roman mosaic floors, stone columns and vaulted, ornate ceilings while keeping exact floorplans under wraps, for fear of terror attacks.

The Bank itself began in rented premises in 1694, moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734. Nicknamed the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street after a satirical cartoon of William Pitt the Younger , it has been refashioned and remodelled – first by Sir John Soane between 1788 and 1833 and then again in the 1920s when the interior was largely demolished and rebuilt.

Cash to fund the scheme will come from an estimated £100m of savings each year for three years that the Bank says will accrue from 450 redundancies and other cost savings. As one member of Bank staff told the Guardian: “It’s like there is a leaving party every week.”

What the Bank wants to avoid is a repeat of the delays and cost overruns that dogged the Federal Reserve in Washington, which led to Trump threatening the US central bank with court action.

Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is now expected to run until December 2027. The final cost is likely to be nearer $2.5bn.

The Bank’s scheme is on a much smaller scale, and pales against the possible £60bn it will cost to renovate the Palace of Westminster . It is more akin to the £80m Elizabeth Tower restoration.

What Bailey will want to avoid is joining the Elizabeth Tower, which houses Big Ben, as the subject of parliamentary scrutiny after its budget doubled and then rose by a further 20% , giving ammunition to critics who have long accused the Bank of mishandling its core purpose of helping to manage the economy by setting interest rates at the appropriate level.

The Bank project was first announced in July 2025 and work was due to start this month, but it was only in October, with a month to spare, that the construction company Sir Robert McAlpine was awarded the building contract.

Described as an “incredibly complex project” , it aims to transform the neoclassical building, which sits opposite the Royal Exchange and adjacent to the Mansion House, into what some staff hope is a Google-like workplace of friendly office spaces, breakout rooms and in-house cafes.

The Bank says there will be no delays, citing the appointment of architects last November. A project manager, a cost consultant and a firm of engineers were also signed up, and they have already begun evaluating budgets and timescales.

A Bank of England spokesperson said: “As part of our plans to preserve our historic Threadneedle Street office we are considering how best to renovate the site and optimise our running costs. All our procurement processes aim to deliver value for money.”

Bailey’s team – based in a grand part of the Bank known as the Parlours – will need to judge the cost implications of meeting new regulations on fire safety, accessibility, electrical testing – with the fire at Notre Dame mid-renovation still fresh in the memory – new plumbing and the need to have a more environmentally friendly building with heating based on renewable sources.

And that’s not to mention the security of the building while all this goes on. Bailey will be concerned that the 400,000 bars of gold, worth more than £200bn, and £100m of bank notes in the vaults are safe from terrorists and thieves.

A further complication is the fate of the Bank’s museum , which is now open to the public and tucked away in the side of the building, facing on to Bartholomew Lane.

Some senior staff had wanted to relocate the museum into the central quad and have the 100,000 visitors a year – mainly schoolchildren – march through the main entrance. Others wanted to have cafe space near the entrance to make the Bank appear more modern and appealing to visitors.

Vivienne Grafton, the executive director of central operations, told the Architects Journal: “This is an opportunity to breathe new life into a legacy building, not through radical reinvention, but through thoughtful, intelligent transformation.”

But architectural plans have yet to be agreed with the local authority – the City of London Corporation – and Historic England, which must sanction the proposed work on a building considered a cornerstone of Britain’s financial district.…

From cashback on what you buy to cut-price gift cards, we offer tips on how to maximise savings on your shopping

With Black Friday on the horizon, retailers are already offering discounts, and over the next few weeks you can expect to see more price cuts as they attempt to entice us to open our wallets.

Assuming you have shopped around for a good price and are sure you really want what you are about to buy, here are some ways you can make the bargain even better.

There are many ways to earn cashback – and you can often stack up more than one.

Some of the big banks pay cashback on purchases made with their debit cards, with offers linked to specific retailers. Lloyds, for example, runs the Rewards programme, which has cashback deals with a rolling cast of retailers. There are similar discount schemes aimed specifically at key workers such as teachers and nurses. These also offer gift cards at below face value.

Three Choirs unveils First Release white wine after long, hot summer led to earliest harvest start in 50 years

F orget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s autumn tradition of opening young wine straight after harvest.

Three Choirs near Newent has unveiled its First Release white wine after the earliest harvest in its 50 years of producing wine.

The First Release is what the vineyard calls its “Gloucestershire nouveau” – its tongue-in-cheek nod to beaujolais nouveau, a young, fruity red that is released on the third Thursday in November . Beaujolais nouveau was traditionally made for local consumption and was a way for workers and villages to enjoy the first sip of that year’s harvest.

Vines were first planted on the Gloucestershire site of a fruit farm in 1973, while Three Choirs has been bottling a young wine every November since the 1980s. Customers can buy the wine directly from the vineyard’s shop or try it in its restaurant.

In the 1980s, the harvest used to begin in mid-September, about a month later than it did this year, according to Three Choir’s winemaking director, Martin Fowke.

This year’s prolonged summer of warm temperatures – and rain at the right time – meant the first grapes were picked on 20 August, a week earlier than the previous record set in 2025. The harvest ended on 9 October, by which time 200 tonnes of grapes had been collected across the vineyard’s 30 hectares (74 acres).

The 2026 First Release is a run of 5,000 bottles of a dry, white wine containing solaris, bacchus, siegerrebe and madeleine angevine grapes.

“We now have an extra month to make the wine. We had riper raw material and longer in the winery,” said Fowke, calling 2026 a “record-breaking year”. He added that higher sugar levels and lower acidity allowed winemakers to make a product that was not possible in Britain 30 years ago.

The early timing of the harvest surprised even the Three Choirs winemaker Jack Abbotts, who was on his summer break when picking started. “It’s usually a safe week for me, but this year it all snowballed,” he said.

The changing climate has made it possible to grow grapes on a commercial scale in Britain, but it also brings challenges.

“We found it hard this year,” said Fowke. “People kept saying: ‘This hot weather must be good for you’, but it was difficult because we knew the heat and lack of rain was challenging for farmers. We don’t need it to get any warmer, that’s for sure.”

Vines have been planted as far north as Yorkshire and Scotland , as Britain’s wine industry expands. More than 1,100 vineyards are now registered in Britain.

While Britain remains far down the list of global wine producers in terms of volume – behind countries including Uzbekistan and Tunisia – it is the fastest-growing wine region in the world , according to the property group Knight Frank. The area of planted vineyards in the country has quadrupled since the turn of the century, it reports.

Some of the newer, smaller vineyards do not have their own winemaking facilities, relying on contract winemakers such as Three Choirs. The Gloucestershire vineyard also produces wine for about 40 others, including Llanerch, located west of Cardiff.

English and Welsh wine producers had their second-largest harvest in 2025, when the equivalent of 16.5m bottles, or 124,377 hectolitres, was produced, according to the industry body WineGB.

The data for the 2026 harvest will not be available until early next year, although WineGB said in August it was “optimistic” about the size and quality after the hot growing season.

If the UK climate continues to change and summers such as 2026’s become the norm, Three Choirs may consider growing new varieties. “We can evolve and change, but we would be planting cabernet sauvignon like they did in Bordeaux 50 years ago,” said Fowke, noting the shift from white to red grapes. “But that is not what we set out to do.”

In the fog and damp of November in Gloucestershire, pruning of the vines ready for the 2027 growing season has already begun. “To have two good years in a row is not uncommon, to have three is unusual,” said Fowke.

You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams.

Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase . On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down . In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack.

But last month, several freezers in France burst into flames after temperature controls in hundreds of shops were hacked , spoiling tons of food and causing an estimated tens of millions of euros of damage. Similar cyber-attacks then hit freezers in six more countries .

Even if the recent outages weren’t the result of malicious behavior, it’s all a visceral reminder that the border between the digital and physical worlds is more porous than ever. And the digital border walls are crumbling – with the AI industry to blame. Frontier AI models can find and exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them, and the rush to patch raises the risk of exactly the kind of disruptions we’re now seeing.

The AI industry is built around relentlessly scaling AI models, discovering what new capabilities emerge, then deploying the models for commercial gain. So far, this process has wrecked education and sloppified the internet; now it threatens to break it altogether.

Instead of waiting to see what the companies break next, we should freeze the reckless gain-of-function experiments they call “frontier AI development”.

Already, hackers are “all using AI now”, declares Ireland’s cybersecurity chief. Google’s top threat analyst agrees : “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited.”

And benefit they have. In recent months, apparent amateurs have used AI to hack more than 100 companies, from the tractor maker Deere to South Korean banks , with the hackers spending as little as $50 per successful infiltration.

Suspected North Korean hackers carried out the biggest heist ever, stealing $6.3bn from the crypto exchange Binance, less than half of which has been frozen or recovered.

Cyber-attacks took down hospital emergency rooms in New Mexico and Germany . AI-enabled hackers broke into the European Commission, disrupting services for more than 10 days.

And on Monday, attackers exploited a flaw in third-party software to serve malware to visitors of 178 organisations’ sites, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom and HSBC.

Last month, researchers using AI discovered a severe flaw in the programming language powering 70% of all websites. (The NSA outage, officials now say , was caused by a rushed patch for that very flaw.) The CEO of internet security provider Cloudflare said he knew of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software … I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

“The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues … is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors,” the CEO of a multi-billion dollar Japanese financial services company said after his company was hacked last month.

While AI has been accelerating cybercrime for years , the recent deluge can be largely attributed to highly capable, easily modified open-weight models released by Chinese developers.

But the AI industry on both sides of the Pacific is responsible for the internet’s “ Black October ” and whatever other cyber horrors await us.

In their quest to render us obsolete , Anthropic and OpenAI were the first to develop and release superhuman hacker AIs – knowing that Chinese developers would piggyback off their progress to release guardrail-free hacker AIs in a matter of months.

The US companies’ plan was to use AI to fix the world’s critical software in time. They didn’t. “I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last month. His new plan is to use AI agents to defend against AI hackers. In other words, the flamethrower industry decided to start selling firehoses too.

When a Twitter/X user told Anthropic’s deputy cyber chief: “You and your cohorts created this monster,” his reply was shockingly candid: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” Thanks for the heads up.

These hacks and disruptions may soon appear quaint. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development”, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in September, “it’s my worry that in 6–12 months [an AI agent] swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet .”

But accelerating AI capabilities aren’t actually a “given” – they’re a product of trillions of dollars in investment and deliberate effort, which is predictably producing enormous new dangers. Anthropic’s IPO filing acknowledges that the entire insurance industry may not be big enough to cover the catastrophic or existential risks the company is creating.

Those risks extend beyond the cyber realm. This summer, researchers at Stanford University synthesized the first AI-designed viruses, and Anthropic quietly set up an automated biology wet lab – a space for physical experiments – in what it says is a bid to find treatments for rare diseases. Meanwhile, AI models steadily improve at assisting in the development of bioweapons. We’ll survive superhuman hacker AIs, but maybe not the bioterrorist variety.

All of these risks will arrive faster if the industry achieves its primary goal: turning AI development over entirely to the machines, in a process known as recursive self-improvement.…

Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

I t’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.

Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.

A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system – and that’s where the core problems lie.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.

Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies – and, additionally, all other positive intangibles – out of a company in pursuit of those profits.

Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.

From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful … until something bad happens.

But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.

The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyber-attack – both human and AI-fueled – and more susceptible to random mistakes.

The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.

We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation – with enforcement and meaningful fines – and stringent antitrust enforcement.

But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement – especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and the University of Toronto’s Munk School

Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

O n Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider , which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset .

“Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director.

One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says.

The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.”

The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.”

He is trying to use fewer pesticides, so is keen to find varieties that are naturally resistant to disease and pests, and will blossom at exactly the moment when spring conditions suit apple tree pollinators such as bumblebees and honeybees.

Another priority is to find varieties that need less winter chill in a warming climate: apple trees, he explains, need a sustained cold period in winter to complete their dormancy, which enables their fruit buds to develop properly in spring. “That winter chill is really important – and last year, we probably didn’t have quite enough, and some varieties are more susceptible to a lack of winter chill than others.”

Thatchers’ orchard manager, Chris Muntz Torres, says jonagold, a cross between golden delicious and a jonathan apple, performed particularly well in trials this year. “They’ve got this vigour, this willingness to grow, whatever the weather.”

He thinks this is because the tree’s vigorous growth above ground is matched by a strong root system. “That’s what we want – a variety that, irrespective of the weather, is robust enough to grow.”

Myrtle Farm has also begun planting wildflower strips in its orchards, to attract insects that prey on pests such as the rosy apple aphid – a strategy that research has shown could save apple growers up to £3,000 a hectare every year and support native pollinators.

Nigel Jenner, head of agronomy for tree fruit at the global fruit producer AM Fresh UK, works with independent apple farmers, who represent about 30% of Britain’s apple-growing industry. He says roughly 70% of these growers – about 220 – have planted wildflower strips in the past five years, and that number is increasing.

“We know this is the way forward,” Jenner says. “It works and it has a meaningful effect on your chemical input and your spray bill.”

He hopes seed producers will soon develop an “orchard mix” of wildflowers designed to attract the beneficial insects that apple growers need, and produce enough of it to bring prices down and make the practice even more widespread.

Many independent growers are also experimenting with new methods of water management, Jenner says. “Years ago, you’d kick the soil and say ‘oh that’s a bit dry, we’ll water it’. Now, we’re using neutron probes to measure the water deficit and we’re trying to get the trees to hunt for water.”

This involves letting the trees become water-stressed, he says: the top 65mm of soil in an orchard is left to dry out, which encourages deeper root growth and reduces the need for irrigation.

Back at Myrtle Farm, Thatchers is also working to improve soil health through regenerative farming. Before any trees are planted in new orchards, herbal leys – mixtures of grasses, legumes and deep-rooted herbs such as chicory – are sown and the land is grazed by sheep.

“Their little feet pound the ground, which improves the soil structure, and they eat the herbal ley and then recycle it very effectively back into the ground, which also improves the soil structure. So where we’ve had fields that have been continuous cereals or maize, we’ve found that within three years, the soil on all the metrics that are important for growing apples improves by at least 20%,” says Thatcher.…

The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa , on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago , when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park , owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy , but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”

Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.

A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
